You are given the following points: A = (10, 12, -16), B = (16, 0, 5), C = (-6, -8, 12).

Which point is closest to the yz-plane?
?
A
B
C
What is the distance from the yz-plane to this point?

Which point is farthest from the xy-plane?
?
A
B
C
What is the distance from the xy-plane to this point?

Which point lies on the xz-plane?
?
A
B
C

solution.p: SOLUTION
The distance from a point to the yz-plane is the absolute value of the x-coordinate.
The point C(-6,-8,12) has the x coordinate with the smallest absolute value, so C is the point closest to the yz- plane.
The distance from the yz-plane to C is given by the absolute value of the x-coordinate, i.e. \left| -6 \right| = 6.
The distance from a point to the xy-plane is the absolute value of the z-coordinate.
The point A(10,12,-16) has the z coordinate with the largest absolute value, so A is the point farthest from the xy- plane.
The distance from the xy-plane to A is given by the absolute value of the z-coordinate, i.e. \left| -16 \right| = 16.
A point lies on the xz-plane if its y-coordinate is zero. Thus B(16,0,5) lies on the xz-plane.

Resolve the following vectors into components:
(a) The vector \vec v in 2-space of length 7 pointing up at an angle of 3\pi/4 measured from the positive x-axis.
\vec v = \vec i + \vec j
(b) The vector \vec w in 3-space of length 5 lying in the yz-plane pointing upward at an angle of 2\pi/3 measured from the positive y-axis.
\vec v = \vec i + \vec j + \vec k

static.solution:
(a) The components are v_1 = 7 \cos 3\pi/4 = (7)(-{1\over\sqrt 2}) = -{7 \over\sqrt 2} and v_2 = 7 \sin 3\pi/4 = (7)({1\over\sqrt 2}) = {7 \over\sqrt 2}. Thus \vec v = -{7 \over\sqrt 2}\,\vec i + {7 \over\sqrt 2}\,\vec j.
(b) Since the vector lies in the yz-plane, its x-component is 0. Its y-component is (5)(\cos 2\pi/3) = -{5 \over 2}, and and its z-component is (5)(\sin 2\pi/3) = {5\sqrt 3 \over 2}. So the vector is \vec w = -{5 \over 2}\,\vec j + {5\sqrt 3 \over 2}\,\vec k.

statement.p: (a) Find a unit vector from the point P=(2,1) and toward the point Q=(10,16).
(b) Find a vector of length 51 pointing in the same direction.

static.solution:
(a) The displacement from P to Q is given by \overrightarrow{PQ} = (10\,\vec i + 16\,\vec j) - (2\,\vec i + 1\,\vec j) = 8\,\mathit{\vec i}+15\,\mathit{\vec j}. Since \mbox{len}{\overrightarrow{PQ}} = \sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} = 17, a unit vector \vec u in the direction of \overrightarrow{PQ} is given by \vec u = \frac{1}{17}\,\overrightarrow{PQ} = \frac{1}{17}\,(8\,\mathit{\vec i}+15\,\mathit{\vec j}) .
(b) A vector of length 51 pointing in the same direction is given by 51\,\vec u = \frac{51}{17}\,(8\,\mathit{\vec i}+15\,\mathit{\vec j}) = 24\,\mathit{\vec i}+45\,\mathit{\vec j}.

solution.p: Vectors are parallel if they are scalar multiples of one another. If we multiply \langle 0.99,-0.12 \rangle by any scalar, it will change its length, making it no longer a unit vector, unless the scalar we choose is 1 or -1. Multiplying by 1 gives us the same vector again, but we were asked for a different one. Thus we must choose -1\cdot\langle 0.99,-0.12 \rangle, which is \langle -0.99,0.12 \rangle.

Consider the wind velocity vectors \vec w_1 = 3\mathit{\vec i}-\mathit{\vec j} \qquad \vec w_2 = -\mathit{\vec i}-3\mathit{\vec j} \qquad \vec w_3 = \mathit{\vec i}+6\mathit{\vec j} \vec w_4 = -8\mathit{\vec i}+2\mathit{\vec j} \qquad \vec w_5 = -4\mathit{\vec i}-\mathit{\vec j}.
Which of the wind velocity vectors increases the plane's speed the most?

Wind

w1
w2
w3
w4
w5

Wind
?
w1
w2
w3

static.solution:
\vec w in the direction of the airplane. A direction vector for the airplane is \vec v = -\mathit{\vec i}-\mathit{\vec j}. The component of \vec w_1 in the direction of \vec v is given by {{\vec w_1 \cdot \vec v} \over ||{\vec v}}|| = {-2 \over \sqrt{2}} \approx -1.41.
Similarly, we find the component for each wind vector in the direction of the airplane. We see that, in the direction of the airplane, the component of \vec w_1 is -1.41, of \vec w_2 is 2.83, of \vec w_3 is -4.95, of \vec w_4 is 4.24, and of \vec w_5 is 3.54.
Thus, the vector \vec w_4 increases the plane's speed the most and the vector \vec w_3 slows the plane down the most.

angle =

solution.p: Let A be one corner of the base, B be the opposite corner on the base, and C be the point that is directly above B on the top of the box. ABC is a right triangle with right angle at B, and AC is its hypotenuse. AC is also a diagonal of the box, and AB is a diagonal of the base of the box. Therefore angle A of this triangle is the angle that we want.

Its cosine is \displaystyle{\begin{aligned} \cos(A) \amp = \frac{\text{length of }AB}{\text{length of }AC} \\ \amp = \frac{\sqrt{18^2+7^2}}{\sqrt{18^2+7^2+4^2}} \end{aligned} } so \displaystyle{A = \arccos\left(\frac{\sqrt{18^2+7^2}}{\sqrt{18^2+7^2+4^2}}\right) \approx {0.204225} \text{ radians}}.

statement.p: The force on an object is \vec F = -22\,\mathit{\vec j}. For the vector \vec v = -3\,\mathit{\vec i}-\,\mathit{\vec j}, find:
(a) The component of \vec F parallel to \vec v:
(b) The component of \vec F perpendicular to \vec v:
The work, W, done by force \vec F through displacement \vec v:

static.solution:
\vec v. Since ||\vec v|| = \sqrt{(-3)^2+(-1)^2} = \sqrt{10}, the unit vector in direction of \vec v is \vec u = \vec v/\sqrt{10}. Then
(a) \vec F_{||} = (\vec F \cdot \vec u) \vec u = (22/\sqrt{10}) \vec u = \frac{-66}{10} \vec i + \frac{-22}{10} \vec j.
(b) We have \vec F_{\perp} = \vec F - \vec F_{||} = (-22\,\mathit{\vec j}) - (\frac{-66}{10} \vec i + \frac{-22}{10} \vec j) \approx 6.6\,\mathit{\vec i}-19.8\,\mathit{\vec j}.
(c) Since work is the dot product of the force and displacement vectors, we have W = \vec F \cdot \vec v = 22.

statement.p: Consider the vectors \vec a = 2\,\mathit{\vec i}+\,\mathit{\vec j}-\,\mathit{\vec k}, \qquad \vec b = - \vec{i} - 2 \vec{j} + \vec{k}, \qquad \vec c = -2\,\mathit{\vec i}-\,\mathit{\vec j}+\,\mathit{\vec k} \vec d = \,\mathit{\vec i}+\,\mathit{\vec j}+3\,\mathit{\vec k},\qquad \vec g = \,\mathit{\vec i}+2\,\mathit{\vec j}-\,\mathit{\vec k}. Which pairs (if any) of these vectors are
(a) Are perpendicular?

p.em: (Enter none or a pair or list of pairs, e.g., if \vec a is perpendicular to \vec b and \vec c, enter (a,b),(a,c).)

statement.p: (b) Are parallel?

p.em: (Enter none or a pair or list of pairs, e.g., if \vec a is parallel to \vec b and \vec c, enter (a,b),(a,c).)

statement.p: (c) Have an angles less than \pi/2 between them?

p.em: (Enter none or a pair or list of pairs, e.g., if \vec a is at an angle less than pi/2 from \vec b and \vec c, enter (a,b),(a,c).)

statement.p: (d) Have an angle of more than \pi/2 between them?

p.em: (Enter none or a pair or list of pairs, e.g., if \vec a is at an angle greater than pi/2 from \vec b and \vec c, enter (a,b),(a,c).)

static.solution:
(a) Perpendicular vectors have a dot product of 0. Since \vec a\cdot\vec d = (2)\cdot(1) + (1)\cdot(1) + (-1)\cdot(3) = 0 and similarly \vec b\cdot\vec d = 0, \vec c\cdot\vec d = 0, \vec d\cdot\vec g = 0, the pairs we want are (\vec a, \vec d), (\vec b, \vec d), (\vec c, \vec d), (\vec d, \vec g).
(b) Parallel vectors are multiples of one another. Since \vec a and \vec c are constant multiples of each other and similarly for \vec b and \vec g, the pairs we want are (\vec a, \vec c), (\vec b, \vec g).
(c) Since \vec v\cdot\vec w= \Vert\vec v\Vert \Vert\vec w\Vert\cos\theta, the dot product of the vectors we want is positive. Since \vec a\cdot\vec g = (2)\cdot(1) + (1)\cdot(2) + (-1)\cdot(-1) > 0 and similarly \vec b\cdot\vec c > 0, the pairs we want are (\vec a, \vec g), (\vec b, \vec c).
(d) Vectors with an angle of more than \pi/2 between them have a negative dot product. Since \vec a\cdot\vec b = (2)\cdot(-1) + (1)\cdot(-2) + (-1)\cdot(1) \lt 0 and similarly \vec a\cdot\vec c \lt 0, \vec b\cdot\vec g \lt 0, \vec c\cdot\vec g \lt 0, the pairs we want are (\vec a, \vec b), (\vec a, \vec c), (\vec b, \vec g), (\vec c, \vec g).

p.m: \text{the paths cross, and the particles collide there}

static.solution:
(2,-4,5) in the direction of the vector \vec i + 2 \vec j - 2 \vec k and the second passes through (-8,-9,10) in the direction of the vector 3 \vec i + 3 \vec j - 3 \vec k. The two paths are not parallel.
Is there a time t when the two particles are at the same place at the same time? If so, then the particles collide, and their coordinates will be the same. Equating coordinates, we get 2 + t = -8 + 3 t, \quad -4 + 2 t = -9 + 3 t,\quad 5 - 2 t = 10 - 3 t.
Since all three equations are solved by t=5, the two particles do in fact arrive at the same place at the same time, and so they do collide.
Then, the two paths cross if there are times t_1 and t_2 such that the position of the first particle at time t_1 is the same as the position of the second particle at time t_2. In this case this is obvious: when t_1 = t_2 = 5, the paths cross.

equation:

static.solution: Both lines are parallel to the x-axis; thus our plane must have x-slope zero. On the other hand, the line in the xy-plane is 6 units down and unit in front of of the line in the y z-plane; hence the y-slope of our plane must be -2. Thus the equation is z = 0 x - 2 y + c, for some constant c. Since the plane contains the point (0,0,6), the value of c must be 6. So the equation is z = -2 y + 6. This is shown in the graph below.

statement.p: (a) Find a vector parallel to the line of intersection of the planes x - y - 2 z = 4 and 5 x - 5 y - 2 z = 12.
(b) Show that the point \left(1,-1,-1\right) lies on both planes. Then find a vector parametric equation for the line of intersection.

static.solution:
(a) Normal vectors to the two planes are \vec n_1 = \vec i - \vec j - 2 \vec k \quad \hbox{ and } \quad \vec n_2 = 5\vec i - 5 \vec j - 2 \vec k. The vector \vec n_1\times\vec n_2 is perpendicular to both planes and parallel to the line of intersection: \vec n_1\times\vec n_2 = \left| \begin{array}{ccc} \vec i \amp \vec j \amp \vec k\\ 1 \amp -1 \amp -2\\ 5 \amp -5 \amp -2 \end{array} \right| = -8\,\mathit{\vec i}-8\,\mathit{\vec j}.
(b) To check that the point \left(1,-1,-1\right) lies on the planes, substitute into each equation. x - y - 2 z = (1)(1) + (-1)(-1) + (-2)(-1) = 4, and 5 x - 5 y - 2 z = (5)(1) + (-5)(-1) + (-2)(-1) = 12. Thus, the point lies on both planes. Then a vector parametric equation of the line is \vec r(t) = \left(1-8t\right)\,\mathit{\vec i}-\left(1+8t\right)\,\mathit{\vec j}-\,\mathit{\vec k}.

statement.p: Evaluate the surface integral \int_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \ d \mathbf{S} where \mathbf{F}=5xy\boldsymbol{i}+6x^{2}\boldsymbol{j}+5yz\boldsymbol{k}\ and S is the surface z=xe^y,\ 0 \le x \le 1, 0 \le y \le 1, with upwards orientation.

static.solution: \mathbf{r}(x,y)=(x,y,g(x,y)) where z = g(x,y) = xe^y and D is the square D = [0,1]\times [0,1]. S has upwards orientation, so \int_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \ d \mathbf{S} = \int\int_D ( -5 x y \frac{\delta g}{\delta x} - 6 x^2 \frac{\delta g}{\delta y} + 5 y z)\ dA = \int\int_D (-5 x y e^y - 6 x^3 e^y + 5 y z)\ dA = \int_0^1\int_0^1 (-5 x y e^y - 6 x^3 e^y + 5 x y e^y)\ dy\ dx = \int_0^1 [- 6 x^3 e^y]_0^1\ dx = \int_0^1 - 6 x^3 (e - 1)\ dx = 6(1 - e)\int_0^1 x^3 \ dx = \frac {3} 2 (1-e)

statement.p: Find a vector \mathbf{n} normal to the plane with the equation 5x+5y+z=7.
\mathbf{n} = \left\lt 5 ,\right., \left.\right>
Find an equation of the plane through the three points given:

static.solution:
\mathbf{n}\cdot \left\lt x,y,z\right>=d
To find the normal vector to the plane, \mathbf{n}, we first compute the vectors \vec{PQ} and \vec{PR} that lie in the plane, and then find the cross product of these vectors. This gives:
\vec{PQ}= \left\lt 4,4,-1\right> - \left\lt 0,0,1\right> = \left\lt 4,4,-2\right>
\vec{PR}= \left\lt -2,1,-2\right> - \left\lt 0,0,1\right> = \left\lt -2,1,-3\right>
\mathbf{n} = \vec{PQ}\times \vec{PR} = \left| \begin{array}{ccc} \boldsymbol{i} \amp \boldsymbol{j} \amp \boldsymbol{k} \\ 4 \amp 4 \amp -2 \\ -2 \amp 1 \amp -3 \end{array} \right|
\qquad = \left| \begin{array}{cc} 4 \amp -2 \\ 1 \amp -3 \end{array} \right| \boldsymbol{i} -\left| \begin{array}{cc} 4 \amp -2 \\ -2 \amp -3 \end{array} \right| \boldsymbol{j} +\left| \begin{array}{cc} 4 \amp 4 \\ -2 \amp 1 \end{array} \right| \boldsymbol{k}
\qquad =-10 \boldsymbol{i} + 16 \boldsymbol{j} + 12 \boldsymbol{k}
We now choose any of the three points in the plane, say P=\left(0,0,1\right), and compute d.
d=\mathbf{n} \cdot\vec{OP}=\left\lt -10,16,12\right> \cdot \left\lt 0,0,1\right> = 12
Finally we obtain the following equation of the plane:
-10 x + 16 y + 12 z = 12.

\left\lt -5,-4,1\right> \cdot \left\lt x,y,z\right> =\left\lt -5,-4,1\right> \cdot \left\lt 0,0,0\right>=0
z-\left(5x+4y\right)=0

statement.p: Find the equation of the ellipsoid passing through the points (\pm 2,0,0),(0,\pm 1,0) and (0,0,\pm 2)
Find the equation of the hyperboloid of one sheet passing through the points (\pm 3,0,0),(0,\pm 7,0) and (\pm 6,0,5),(0,\pm 14,5)

static.solution:
z=z_{0} are ellipses. Hence, the equation of the hyperboloid has the form
\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^2-\left(\frac{z}{c}\right)^2=1
Substituting z=0 we get
\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^2=1
By the given information this ellipse has x and y intercepts at the points (\pm 3,0),(0,\pm 7). So we get
\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{y}{7}\right)^2-\left(\frac{z}{c}\right)^2=1
Substituting z=5 we get
\frac{x^2}{3^2} + \frac{y^2}{7^2} -\frac{5^2}{c^2}=1
\frac{x^2}{9} + \frac{y^2}{49} =1+\frac{25}{c^2}=\frac{c^2+25}{c^2}
\frac{c^2 x^2}{9(c^2+25)} + \frac{c^2 y^2}{49(c^2+25)} = 1
\left(\frac{x}{\frac{3}{c}\sqrt{c^2+25}}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{y}{\frac{7}{c}\sqrt{c^2+25}}\right)^2=1
By the given information the following must hold: \frac{3}{c}\sqrt{c^2+25}=6 and \frac{7}{c}\sqrt{c^2+25}=14
\frac{\sqrt{c^2+25}}{c}=2, so c^2+25=4c^2 and 3c^2=25
Thus, c=\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}, and by substituting we obtain the following equation
\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{y}{7}\right)^2-\left(\frac{z}{\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}}\right)^2=1

solution.p: SOLUTION
1. Completing the squares, yields (x-2)^2+(y-2)^2+(z-1)^2 = \frac{1}{4}. Thus the sphere is centered at (2,2,1) and has radius \frac{1}{2}. Its graph matches D.
2. The sphere is centered at (0,0,-1) and has radius \frac{3}{2}. Thus it matches C.
3. Completing the squares, yields (x-1)^2+(y+1)^2+(z-1)^2 = 1. Thus the sphere is centered at (1,-1,1) and has radius 1. Its graph matches E.
4. The sphere is centered at the origin and it has radius 2. Thus it matches A.

statement.p: Convert from rectangular to polar coordinates:
Note: Choose r and \theta such that r is nonnegative and 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi
\mathbf{(a)}\quad (2,0)\quad\Rightarrow_{(r,\theta)}\quad(,)
\mathbf{(b)}\quad(12,\frac{12}{\sqrt{3}})\quad\Rightarrow_{(r,\theta)}\quad(,)
\mathbf{(c)}\quad(-3,3)\quad\Rightarrow_{(r,\theta)}\quad(,)
\mathbf{(d)}\quad(-\sqrt{3},1)\quad\Rightarrow_{(r,\theta)}\quad(,)

static.solution:
\mathbf{(a)} The point (2,0) is on the positive x axis distanced 2 units from the origin. Hence, r=2 and \theta=0.
Thus, (r,\theta)=(2,0)
\mathbf{(b)} The point (12,\frac{12}{\sqrt{3}}) is in the first quadrant so \theta = \tan^{-1} \left(\frac{\frac{12}{\sqrt{3}}}{12}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}.
Also, r=\sqrt{{12}^2+\left({\frac{12}{\sqrt{3}}}\right)^2} = \sqrt{192} Hence, (r,\theta)=\left(\sqrt{192},\frac{\pi}{6}\right)
\mathbf{(c)} The point (-3,3) is in the second quadrant. Hence, { \theta ={ \tan}^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{-3}\right) = {\tan}^{-1}(-1)=\pi -\frac{\pi }{4}=\frac{3\pi }{4}}. Also, r=\sqrt{{(-3)}^{2}+{3}^{2}}=\sqrt{18}. Hence, \left(r,\theta\right)=\left(\sqrt{18},\frac{3\pi }{4}\right).
\mathbf{(d)} The point \left(-\sqrt{3},1\right) is in the second quadrant, hence, \theta ={\tan}^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{-\sqrt{3}}\right)= \tan^{-1}\left(-\frac1{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\pi -\frac{\pi }{6}=\frac{5\pi }{6}. Also, r=\sqrt{\left(-\sqrt{3}\right)^{2}+{\left(1\right)}^{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2. Hence, \left(r,\theta \right)=\left(2,\frac{5\pi }{6}\right).

statement.p: Convert from polar to rectangular coordinates:
\mathbf{(a)}\quad(3,\frac{\pi}{3})\quad\Rightarrow_{(x,y)}\quad(,)
\mathbf{(b)}\quad(3,\frac{\pi}{2})\quad\Rightarrow_{(x,y)}\quad(,)
\mathbf{(c)}\quad(6,\frac{\pi}{4})\quad\Rightarrow_{(x,y)}\quad(,)

static.solution:
\mathbf{(a)} Since r=3 and \theta =\frac{\pi}{3}, we have: x=r\cos\theta=3\cos \frac{\pi}{3}=3\cdot \frac12=1.5 y=r\sin\theta=3\sin \frac{\pi}{3}=3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=2.59808 \Downarrow (x,y)=(1.5,2.59808)
\mathbf{(b)} For (3,\frac{\pi}{2}) we have r=3 and \theta=\frac{\pi}{2}. Hence, x=r\cos\theta=3\cos \frac{\pi}{2}=3\cdot 0=0 y=r\sin\theta=3\sin \frac{\pi}{2}=3\cdot 1=3 \Downarrow (x,y)=(0,3)
\mathbf{(c)} Since r=6 and \theta =\frac{\pi}{4}, we have: x=r\cos\theta=6\cos \frac{\pi}{4}=6\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=4.24264 y=r\sin\theta=6\sin \frac{\pi}{4}=6\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=4.24264 \Downarrow (x,y)=(4.24264,4.24264)

statement.p: Which of the following two equations defines a horizontal line?
Write "T" if the equation defines a horizontal line, "F" otherwise.

static.solution:
r=6 \csc \theta is the polar equation of a horizontal line, as it can be written as r=6/\sin \theta, so r \sin \theta = 6, which becomes y=6.
On the other hand, the equation r=6 \sec \theta is the polar equation of a vertical line, as it can be written as r=6/\cos \theta, so r \cos \theta = 6, which becomes x=6.

statement.p: The following polar equation describes a circle in rectangular coordinates: r = 12\sin\theta Locate its center on the xy-plane, and find the circle's radius.

static.solution: r and substituting y =r \sin \theta and {r}^{2}={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} gives {r}^{2}=12 r \sin \theta \Rightarrow {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=12 y We complete the square to obtain {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-12 y=0 x^2+{\left(y-6\right)}^{2}={6}^{2} Thus, r=12 \sin \theta is the equation of a circle of radius 6 and center \left(0,6\right).

Convert the following point from rectangular to cylindrical coordinates: (4\sqrt{2},-4\sqrt{2},-7).
Usage: To enter a point, for example (x,y,z), type "(x, y, z)".

static.solution:
(x,y,z)=(4\sqrt{2},-4\sqrt{2},-7). We first find r: r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=\sqrt{(4\sqrt{2})^2+(-4\sqrt{2})^2}=8. Since the point (x,y)=(4\sqrt{2},-4\sqrt{2}) lies in the fourth quadrant, \frac{3\pi}{2}\leq \theta\leq 2\pi. Hence \tan \theta=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{-4\sqrt{2}}{4\sqrt{2}}=-1, so \theta=\frac{7 \pi}{4}.
The cylindrical coordinates are thus (r,\theta,z)=\left( 8, \frac{7 \pi}{4}, -7 \right).

statement.p: Convert the following point from spherical to rectangular coordinates: \left(3, \frac{ \pi}{3}, \frac{5 \pi}{3}\right).
Usage: To enter a point, for example (x,y,z), type "(x, y, z)".
Convert the following point from rectangular to spherical coordinates: \left(\frac{ 3\sqrt{2}}{4},\frac{ 3\sqrt{6}}{4},\frac{ 3\sqrt{2}}{2}\right).
Usage: To enter a point, for example (x,y,z), type "(x, y, z)".

static.solution:
x=\frac{ 3\sqrt{2}}{4}, y=\frac{ 3\sqrt{6}}{4}, and z=\frac{ 3\sqrt{2}}{2}. The radial coordinate is \rho=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}=\sqrt{\textstyle \left(\frac{ 3\sqrt{2}}{4}\right)^2+\left(\frac{ 3\sqrt{6}}{4}\right)^2+\left(\frac{ 3\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)^2}=3. The angular coordinate \theta satisfies \tan \theta=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{ 3\sqrt{6}/4}{ 3\sqrt{2}/4}=\sqrt{3} so either \theta=\frac{ \pi}{3} or \theta=\frac{4 \pi}{3}. Since the point (x,y)=(\frac{ 3\sqrt{2}}{4},\frac{ 3\sqrt{6}}{4}) is in the first quadrant, the correct choice is \theta=\frac{ \pi}{3}. The angle of declination \phi satisfies \cos \phi=\frac{z}{\rho}=\frac{ \sqrt{2}}{2}, \qquad 0\leq \phi\leq \pi and so \phi=\frac{ \pi}{4}.
The spherical coordinates are thus (\rho,\theta,\phi)=\left(3,\frac{ \pi}{3},\frac{ \pi}{4}\right).

li.p: A parametrization of the graph of y = \ln(x) for x > 0 is given by x = e^t, y = t for -\infty \lt t \lt \infty.
The line parametrized by x = 7, y = 5t, z = 6 + t is parallel to the x-axis.
The parametric curve x = (3t+4)^2, y = 5(3t+4)^2-9, for 0 \leq t \leq 3 is a line segment.

solution.p: SOLUTION
1. Substituting x = e^t, y = t into the equation y= \ln(x) yields t = \ln(e^t) = t. For the given values of t, x > 0. Thus the statement is True.
2. The direction vector of the line is \langle 0, 5, 1\rangle. This vector is not parallel to the x-axis. Thus the statement is False.
3. Eliminating the parameter t yields the equation y = 5x -9,\; 16 \le x \le 169. Thus the parametric curve is a line segment and the statement is True.

static.solution: z is constant since the curve is parallel to the xy-plane, so z=-2 since it passes through (0,3,-2). One possible answer is x = t-1, \quad y = 3-5\mathopen{}\left(t-1\right)^{4}, \quad z=-2, which passes through the indicated point, with x'(1)=1.

statement.p: Find parametric equations for the arc of a circle of radius 5 from P=(0,0) to Q=(10,0).
with \le t\le

static.solution: PQ has length 10, so it must be a diameter of the circle. The center of the circle is therefore the midpoint of PQ, which is the point (5,0). The upper arc of the circle between P and Q can be parameterized as follows: \vec r (t) = 5\vec i + 5(-\cos t \vec i + \sin t \vec j), \quad 0 \le t \le \pi. The lower arc can be parameterized as follows: \vec r (t) = 5\vec i + 5(\cos t \vec i + \sin t \vec j), \quad \pi \le t \le 2\pi.

statement.p: A particle moves on a circle of radius 6 cm, centered at the origin, in the xy-plane (x and y measured in centimeters). At time t=0 it starts at the point (0,6) and moves counterclockwise as t increases, going once around the circle in 8 seconds at constant speed.
(a) Write a parameterization for the particle's motion.
(b) What is the particle's speed?
speed =

p.em: (Give .)

static.solution:
(a) For any positive constant k, the parameterization x=-6\sin(kt)\quad y=6\cos(kt) moves counterclockwise on a circle of radius 6 starting at the point (0,6). We choose k to make the period 8 seconds. If k\cdot 8=2\pi, then k=\pi/4 and the parameterization is x=-6\sin\left(\frac {\pi t}{4}\right)\qquad y=6\cos \left(\frac {\pi t}{4}\right).
(b) Since it takes 8 seconds for the particle to go around the circle \mbox{Speed}=\frac{\mbox{Circumference of circle}}{8} = \frac {2\pi(6)}{8} = \frac {3\pi}{2}\mbox{ cm/sec}.

statement.p: Suppose a curve is traced by the parametric equations x = 4 \big(\sin(t)+\cos(t)\big)
as t runs from 0 to \pi. At what point (x,y) on this curve is the tangent line horizontal?

static.solution:
0 = \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \frac{20\cdot 2\cos(t)\sin(t) - 40\cos(t)}{4 \big(\cos(t)-\sin(t)\big)}.
If this fraction is zero then its numerator is zero 0=dy/dt = 40\cos(t)\big(\sin(t)-1\big) so \cos(t)=0 or \sin(t)=1. Since 0\leq t \leq \pi it follows that t = \frac{\pi}{2} is the only possibility. It works because the denominator of the fraction \displaystyle \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} is not zero when t=\pi/2, so there really is a horizontal tangent when t=\pi/2.
Plug t=\pi/2 into the parametric equations to obtain x,y-coordinates of the point where the horizontal line is tangent x= 4 \left(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)+\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right)= 4 and y = 41 - 20\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) - 40\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 41 - 0 - 40 = 1.

statement.p: Determine whether {\bf r}_1 and {\bf r}_2 collide or intersect:

The two paths
do not collide

The two paths

intersect

static.solution:
t such that:

Equating corresponding components we obtain the following equations:
t=5t+1

t^3=216
The second equation implies that t=0, but this value does not satisfy the other equations. Therefore, the equations have no solution, which means that the paths do not collide.
The two paths intersect if there exist values of t and s such that:
\left\lt s,s^2,s^3 \right> = \left\lt 5t+1, 36t^{2},216 \right>
Or equivalently:
s=5t+1
s^2=36t^{2}
s^3=216
The second equation implies that s=\pm 6 t, and the third equation implies s=6. Hence t=\pm 1
We can see that one of the solutions satisfies the first equation, hence the two paths intersect.

A child wanders slowly down a circular staircase from the top of a tower. With x,y,z in feet and the origin at the base of the tower, her position t minutes from the start is given by x=10\cos t,\quad y = 10 \sin t, \quad z = 90 - 5 t.
(a) How tall is the tower?
height = ft
(b) When does the child reach the bottom?
time = minutes
(c) What is her speed at time t?
speed = ft/min
(d) What is her acceleration at time t?
acceleration = ft/min{}^2

static.solution:
(a) Since z=90 feet when t=0, the tower is 90 feet high.
(b) The child reaches the bottom when z=0, so t=90/5=18 minutes.
(c) Her velocity is given by \vec v =\frac{d\vec r}{dt} = -(10\sin t)\vec i +(10\cos t)\vec j - 5\vec k, so \hbox{Speed} = ||\vec v|| = \sqrt{(-10\sin t)^2+(10\cos t)^2 + (-5)^2} = \sqrt{10^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{125} \mbox{ ft/min}.
(c) Her acceleration is given by \vec a = \frac{d\vec v}{dt} = -(10 \cos t)\vec i -(10 \sin t)\vec j \mbox{ ft/min}^2.

Usage: To enter a vector, for example \langle x,y,z\rangle, type \lt x, y, z \gt

static.solution: \mathbf{a}(t) to obtain the velocity vector: \mathbf{v}(t) = \int_0^t \left\lt u,9\right> du = \left.\left\langle \frac{u^2}{2},9 u\right\rangle\right|_0^t+\mathbf{v}_0 = \left\langle \frac{t^2}{2},9 t\right\rangle+\mathbf{v}_0. The initial condition \mathbf{v}(0)=\left\lt -2,3\right> gives: \mathbf{v}(0) = \langle 0,0\rangle+\mathbf{v}_0=\left\lt -2,3\right> so \mathbf{v}_0=\left\lt -2,3\right> and we obtain \mathbf{v}(t) = \left\langle \frac{t^2}{2},9 t\right\rangle+\left\lt -2,3\right> = \left\langle \frac{t^2}{2} - 2,9 t+3\right\rangle. We now integrate the velocity vector to find \mathbf{r}(t): \begin{array}{rcl} \mathbf{r}(t) \amp =\amp \displaystyle\int_0^t \left\langle \frac{u^2}{2} - 2,9 u+3\right\rangle\ du \\ \amp =\amp \left.\left\langle \frac{u^3}{6} - 2 u,\frac{9 u^2}{2}+3 u\right\rangle\right|_0^t +\mathbf{r}_0 \\ \amp =\amp \left\langle \frac{t^3}{6} - 2 t,\frac{9 t^2}{2}+3 t\right\rangle+\mathbf{r}_0 \end{array} The initial condition \mathbf{r}(0)=\langle 0,0\rangle gives \mathbf{r}_0=\langle 0,0\rangle, so \mathbf{r}(t)=\left\langle \frac{t^3}{6} - 2 t,\frac{9 t^2}{2}+3 t\right\rangle.

\bf r\it'(t) to find the general solution:
\bf r\it(t)=\int \left\lt \sin 2 t,\sin 9 t,3 t\right> \,dt
= \left\lt \int \sin 2 t dt,\int \sin 9 t dt,\int 3 t dt\right> = \left\lt -\frac{1}{2}\cos 2 t,-\frac{1}{9}\cos 9 t,\frac{3}{2} t^2\right> + \bf c\it Substituting the initial condition we obtain:
\bf r\it(0)=\left\lt -\frac{1}{2}\cos 0,-\frac{1}{9}\cos 0,\frac{3}{2} 0^2\right> + \bf c\it
= \left\lt 9,9,8\right> = \left\lt -\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{9},0\right> + \bf c\it Hence,
\bf c\it=\left\lt 9,9,8\right> - \left\lt -\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{9},0\right> = \left\lt \frac{19}{2},\frac{82}{9},8\right> Hence the solution to the differential equation with the given initial condition is:

Find a path that traces the circle in the plane y=-3 with radius r=5 and center (-3,-3,0) with constant speed 30.
{\bf r\it_1(s)}=\left\lt \right. ,, \left. \right>

static.solution:
\bf r\it(t)=\left\lt -3,-3,0\right>+5\left\lt \cos t,0,\sin t\right>=\left\lt -3+5\cos t, -3, 0+5\sin t\right>
We need to reparametrize the curve by making a substitution on t=\phi(s), so that the new parametrization \bf r\it_1(s)=\bf r\it(\phi(s)) satisfies ||\bf r\it_1'(s)||=30 for all s. We find \bf r\it_1' using the Chain Rule:
\bf r\it_1'(s)=\frac{d}{ds}\bf r\it(\phi(s))=\phi'(s)\bf r\it'(\phi(s))
Next, we differentiate \bf r\it(t) and then replace t by \phi(s):
\bf r\it'(t)=\left\lt -5\sin t, 0, 5\cos t\right>
\bf r\it'(\phi(s))=\left\lt -5\sin(\phi(s)), 0, 5\cos(\phi(s))\right>
Now, we get: \bf r\it_1'(s)=\phi'(s)\left\lt -5\sin(\phi(s)), 0, 5\cos(\phi(s))\right>=5\phi'(s)\left\lt -\sin(\phi(s)), 0,\cos(\phi(s))\right>
Hence,
||\bf r\it_1'(s)||=5|\phi'(s)|\sqrt{(-\sin(s))^2+(\cos(s))^2}=5|\phi'(s)|
To satisfy ||\bf r\it_1'(s)||=30 for all s, we choose \phi'(s)=6.
We may take the antiderivative of \phi(s)=6 s and obtain the following parametrization:
\bf r\it_1(s)=\bf r\it(\phi(s))=r(6 s)=\left\lt -3+5\cos (6 s), -3, 0+5\sin (6 s)\right>

statement.p: Evaluate the integral:
\int_{0}^{t} (5 s {\bf i} + 6 s^2 {\bf j} + 16 {\bf k}) \,ds Answer : {\bf i} \, +{\bf j} \, +{\bf k}

static.solution:
\int_{0}^{t} 5 s \,ds = \left.\frac{5}{2} s^{2}\right|_{0}^{t}= \frac{5}{2} t^2 \int_{0}^{t} 6 s^2 \,ds = \left.\frac{6}{3} s^{3}\right|_0^t= 2 t^3 \left.\int_{0}^{t} 16 \,ds = 16 s\right|_0^t=16 t Hence,
\int_{0}^{t} (5 s \bf{i}\it + 6 s^2 \bf{j}\it + 16 \bf{k}\it) \,ds = \left(\int_{0}^{t} 5 s \,ds\right) \bf{i}\it + \left(\int_{0}^{t} 6 s^2 \,ds\right) \bf{j}\it + \left(\int_{0}^{t} 16 \,ds\right) \bf{k}\it
=\left(\frac{5}{2} t^2\right)\bf{i}\it + \left(2 t^3\right) \bf{j}\it + \left(16 t\right) \bf{k}\it

Find an arc length parametrization \bf r\it_1(s) of {\bf r}({\it t})=\left\lt e^{t}\sin\mathopen{}\left(t\right),e^{t}\cos\mathopen{}\left(t\right),5e^{t}\right>.
Assume t(s)=0 when s=0, and t'(0)>0.
{\bf r\it_1(s)}=\left\lt \right. ,, \left. \right>

static.solution:
\bf r\it_1(s)=\bf r\it(\phi(s)) where t=\phi(s) is the inverse of the arc length function. We compute the arc length function:
s(t)=\int^{t}_{0}||\bf r\it'(u)|| du
Differentiating \bf r\it(t) and computing the norm of \bf r\it'(t) gives:
\bf r\it'(t)=\left\lt e^t\sin t+e^t\cos t, e^t\cos t-e^t\sin t, 5e^{t}\right>
=e^t\left\lt \sin t+\cos t, \cos t-\sin t, 5\right>
||\bf r\it'(t)||=e^t\sqrt{(\sin t+\cos t)^2+(\cos t-\sin t)^2+5^2}=e^t\sqrt{2(\sin^2t+\cos^2t)+25}=\sqrt{27}e^t
Thus,
s(t)=\int^{t}_{0}\sqrt{27}e^udu=\sqrt{27}\left.e^u\right|^{t}_{0}=\sqrt{27}\left(e^t-1\right)
We find the inverse function of s(t) by solving s=\sqrt{27}\left(e^t-1\right) for t. We obtain:
\frac{s}{\sqrt{27}}=e^t-1
e^t=1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{27}}
t=\phi(s)=\ln\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{27}}\right)
Thus arc length parametrization for \bf r\it_1(s)=\bf r\it(\phi(s)) is:
\left\lt \left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{27}}\right)\sin\mathopen{}\left(\ln\mathopen{}\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{27}}\right)\right), \left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{27}}\right)\cos\mathopen{}\left(\ln\mathopen{}\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{27}}\right)\right), 5\mathopen{}\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{27}}\right)\right>
=(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{27}})\left\lt \sin\left(\ln\mathopen{}\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{27}}\right)\right), \cos\left(\ln\mathopen{}\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{27}}\right)\right), 5\right>

static.solution:
L=\int^{\sqrt{45}}_{0}||\bf r\it'(t)dt||
Differentiating \bf r\it(t) and computing the norm of \bf r\it'(t) gives:

||{\bf r}{\it'(t)}||=\sqrt{36 t^2 + 9 t^4}
=t\sqrt{36+9 t^2}, on t\ge 0
Thus,

Integrating (using the substitution u=t^2) we get

= 335

statement.p: Calculate the length of the path over the given interval. c(t) = (5 t^2, 10 t^3), \, 2 \le t \le 3

static.solution: x = 5 t^2 and y = 10 t^3. Hence x' = 10 t and y' = 30 t^2. By the formula for the arc length we get S = \int ^{3} _{2} \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2} \, dt = \int ^{3} _{2} \sqrt{100 t^2 + 900 t^4} \, dt = 10 \int ^{3} _{2} \sqrt{1 + 9 t^2} \, t \, dt Using the substitution u = 1 + 9 t^2, \, du = 18 t \, dt we obtain S = \frac{10}{18} \int ^{82} _{37} \sqrt{u} \, du = \frac{10}{18} \cdot \frac{2}{3} u^{3/2} \mid ^{82} _{37} = \frac{20}{54} ((82)^{3/2} - (37)^{3/2}) = 191.659

statement.p: Calculate the length of the path over the given interval. (\sin 9 t, \cos 9 t), \, 0 \le t \le \pi

static.solution: x = \sin 9 t, \, y = \cos 9 t, hence x' = 9 \cos 9 t and y' = - 9 \sin 9 t. By the formula for the arc length we obtain: S = \int ^\pi _0 \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2} \, dt = \int ^\pi _0 \sqrt{81 \cos^2 9 t + 81 \sin^2 9 t} \, dt = \int ^\pi _0 \sqrt{81} \, dt = 9 \pi

statement.p: Calculate the length of the path over the given interval. (\sin \theta - \theta \cos \theta, \cos \theta + \theta \sin \theta), \, 0 \le \theta \le 2

static.solution: x = \sin \theta - \theta \cos \theta and y = \cos \theta + \theta \sin \theta. Hence, x' = \cos \theta - \left( \cos \theta - \theta \sin \theta \right) = \theta \sin \theta and y' = - \sin \theta + \sin \theta + \theta \cos \theta = \theta \cos \theta. Using the formula for the arc length we obtain: S = \int ^{2} _0 \sqrt{x'(\theta)^2 + y'(\theta)^2} \, dt = \int ^{2} _0 \sqrt{ \left( \theta \sin \theta \right) ^2 + \left( \theta \cos \theta \right)^2 } \, d \theta = \int ^{2} _0 \sqrt{ \theta^2 \left( \sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta \right) } \, d \theta = \int ^{2} _0 \theta \, d \theta = \frac{\theta^2}{2} \mid ^{2} _0 = \frac{4}{2} = 2

statement.p: Find the length of the spiral c(t) = (t \cos t, t \sin t) for 0 \le t \le 2 \pi to three decimal places. Hint: use the formula \int \sqrt{1 + t^2} \, dt = \frac{1}{2} t \sqrt{1 + t^2} + \frac{1}{2} \ln \left( t + \sqrt{1 + t^2} \right) + C

static.solution: S = \int ^{2 \pi} _0 \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2} \, dt Differentiating x = t \cos t and y = t \sin t yields x'(t) = \frac{d}{dt} (t \cos t) = \cos t - t \sin t y'(t) = \frac{d}{dt} (t \sin t) = \sin t + t \cos t Thus, \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2} = \sqrt{(\cos t - t \sin t)^2 + (\sin t + t \cos t)^2} = \sqrt{\cos^2 t - 2 t \cos t \sin t + t^2 \sin^2 t + \sin^2 t + 2 t \sin t \cos t + t^2 \cos^2 t} = \sqrt{(\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t)(1 + t^2)} = \sqrt{1 + t^2} We substitute into (1) and use the integral given in the hint to obtain the following arc length: S = \int ^{2 \pi} _0 \sqrt{1 + t^2} \, dt = \frac{1}{2} t \sqrt{1 + t^2} + \frac{1}{2} \ln \left( t + \sqrt{1 + t^2} \right) \mid ^{2 \pi} _0 = \left[\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \pi \sqrt{1 + (2 \pi)^2} + \frac{1}{2} \ln \left(2 \pi + \sqrt{1 + (2 \pi)^2} \right)\right] - \left[ 0 + \frac{1}{2} \ln 1 \right] = 1 \pi \sqrt{1 + 4 \pi^2} + \frac{1}{2} \ln \left( 2 \pi + \sqrt{1 + 4 \pi^2} \right) \approx 21.256

HINT: use the formula \int \sqrt{ t^2 + a^2} \, dt = \frac{1}{2} t \sqrt{t^2+a^2} + \frac{1}{2} a^2 \ln \left( t + \sqrt{t^2+a^2} \right) + C

static.solution:
\bf r\it(t) is \bf r\it'(t)=6 {\bf \, i}+3{\bf \, j}+2t{\bf \, k}.Using the Arc Length Formula we get: L = \int_0^{3} \left||\bf r\it'(t)\right||\,dt =\int_0^{3} \sqrt{{6}^2+{3}^2+(2t)^2}\,dt =\int_0^{3}\sqrt{4t^2+45}\,dt We substitute u=2t, \,du=2\,dt and use the given integration formula. This gives: L=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{6}\sqrt{u^2+45}\,du= \left.\frac{1}{4}u\sqrt{u^2+45}+\frac{1}{4}\cdot 45\ln\left(u+\sqrt{u^2+45}\right)\right|_0^{6}=
\frac{1}{4}6\sqrt{{6}^2+45}+\frac{45}{4}\ln\left(6+\sqrt{{6}^2+45}\right) - \frac{45}{4}\ln\sqrt{45}
=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{81}+\frac{45}{4}\ln\left(6+\sqrt{81}\right) - \frac{45}{4}\ln\sqrt{45}=
\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{81}+\frac{45}{4}\ln\frac{6+\sqrt{81}}{\sqrt{45}} \approx 22.55

statement.p: Sketch a contour diagram of each function. Then, decide whether its contours are predominantly lines, parabolas, ellipses, or hyperbolas.

solution.p: SOLUTION
1. The contours have equation k = y-4 x^2 , which represent parabolas in the xy- plane.
2. The contours have equation k = -3 x^2. For k \le 0, these equations are equivalent to x = \pm \sqrt{-k/3}, which represent vertical lines in the xy- plane.
3. The contours have equation k = x^2- 3 y^2 , which represent hyperbolas in the xy- plane.
4. The contours have equation k = x^2+ 4 y^2 , which (for k >0) represent ellipses in the xy- plane.

Consider the concentration, C, in mg per liter (L), of a drug in the blood as a function of x, the amount, in mg, of the drug given and t, the time in hours since the injection. For 0 \leq x \leq 3 and t \geq 0, we have C = f(x,t) = t e^{-t(4-x)}.
Graph the following two single variable functions on a separate page, being sure that you can explain their significance in terms of drug concentration.
Using your graph in (a), where is f(1,t)
a maximum? t =
a minimum? t =
Using your graph in (b), where is f(x,3)
a maximum? x =
a minimum? x =

static.solution:
(a) Holding x fixed at 1 means that we are considering an injection of 1 mg of the drug; letting t vary means we are watching the effect of this dose as time passes. Thus the function f(1,t) describes the concentration of the drug in the blood resulting from a 1 mg injection as a function of time. The figure below shows the graph of f(1,t)=t\,e^{-3 t}. Notice that the concentration in the blood from this dose is at a maximum at 0.333333 hour after injection, and that the concentration in the blood eventually approaches zero. The initial concentration is 0, so the minimum occurs at t = 0.
(b) Holding t fixed at 3 means that we are focusing on the blood 3 hours after the injection; letting x vary means we are considering the effect of different doses at that instant. Thus, the function f(x,3) gives the concentration of the drug in the blood 3 hours after injection as a function of the amount injected. The figure below shows the graph of f(x,3)=3 e^{-(4-x)}. Notice that f(x,3) is an increasing function of x. This makes sense: If we administer more of the drug, the concentration in the bloodstream is higher. In particular, this means that the maximum concentration occurs at the maximum value of x, 3, and the minimum at x = 0.

(a) Suppose that we consider (x,y)\to (0,0) along the curve y = 2 x^2. Find the limit in this case:
(b) Now consider (x,y)\to (0,0) along the curve y = 3 x^2. Find the limit in this case:
(c) Note that the results from (a) and (b) indicate that f has no limit as (x,y)\to (0,0) (be sure you can explain why!).
To show this more generally, consider (x,y)\to (0,0) along the curve y = m x^2, for arbitrary m. Find the limit in this case:

p.em: (Be sure that you can explain how this result also indicates that f has no limit as (x,y)\to(0,0).

static.solution:
f does not have a limit as (x,y) approaches (0,0).
(a) If (x,y) tends to (0,0) along the curve y = 2 x^2, then f(x,y) = f(x,2 x^2) = \frac{4x^{2}-2x^{2}}{x^{2}+2x^{2}} = \frac{2}{3}.
Therefore \lim_{x\to0} f(x,2 x^2) = \frac{2}{3}.
(b) Similarly, if (x,y) tends to (0,0) along the curve y = 3 x^2, then f(x,y) = f(x,3 x^2) = \frac{4x^{2}-3x^{2}}{x^{2}+3x^{2}} = \frac{1}{4},
and so \lim_{x\to0} f(x,3 x^2) = \frac{1}{4}.
Because we have two different values for these limits, we know that the function doesn't have a limit at (0,0). No matter how close we are to the origin, there will be points on f(x,y) that are close to \frac{2}{3} and points that are close to \frac{1}{4}, whereas for the limit to exist the function must get close to a single value.
(c) We can see this more generally by considering the limit as (x,y) tends to (0,0) along the curve y = m x^2. Then f(x,y) = f(x,m x^2) = \frac{4-m}{1+m}, so that \lim_{x\to0} f(x,m x^2) = \frac{4-m}{1+m}, and we see for every different value of m we will get a different limiting value for the function. Thus the function does not have a limit at (0,0).

statement.p: Show that the function f(x,y) = \frac{x^{5}y}{x^{10}+y^{5}}. does not have a limit at (0,0) by examining the following limits.
(a) Find the limit of f as (x,y) \to (0,0) along the line y = x.
(b) Find the limit of f as (x,y)\to(0,0) along the curve y = x^5.

p.em: (Be sure that you are able to explain why the results in (a) and (b) indicate that f does not have a limit at (0,0)!

static.solution:
(a) Let us suppose that (x,y) approaches (0,0) along the line y=x. Then f(x,y) = f(x,x) = \frac{x^6}{x^{10} + x^5} = \frac{x}{x^5+1}. Therefore \lim_{^{(x,y)\to(0,0)}_{y=x}} f(x,y) = \lim_{x\to0} \frac{x}{x^5+1} = 0.
(b) On the other hand, if (x,y) approaches (0,0) along the curve y=x^5 we have f(x,y)=f(x,x^5) = \frac{x^{10}}{x^{10} + x^{25}} = 1 and so \lim_{^{(x,y)\to(0,0)}_{y=x^5}} f(x,y) = \lim_{x\to0}f(x,x^5) = 1.
Thus no matter how close they are to the origin, there will be points (x,y) such that f(x,y) is close to 0 and points (x,y) such that f(x,y) is close to 1. So the limit \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)} f(x,y) does not exist.

statement.p: An experiment to measure the toxicity of formaldehyde yielded the data in the table below. The values show the percent, P=f(t,c), of rats surviving an exposure to formaldehyde at a concentration of c (in parts per million, ppm) after t months.
(a) Estimate f_t(20,6):
(b) Estimate f_c(20,6):

p.em: (Be sure that you can give the practical meaning of these two values in terms of formaldehyde toxicity.)

static.solution:
f(20,6) = 90.
(a) Thus, to estimate f_t(20,6), we can take f_t(20,6) \approx \frac{f(20+2,6) - f(20-2,6)}{4} = \frac{86 - 93}{4} = -1.75. Alternately, we could take either of the two one-sided difference quotients, f_t(20,6) \approx \frac{f(20+2,6) - f(20,6)}{2} = -2 or f_t(20,6) \approx \frac{f(20,6) - f(20-2,6)}{2} = -1.5. In each case, the units of f_t are percent per month. This says 20 months after rats are exposed to a formaldehyde concentration of 6 ppm, the percent of rats surviving is decreasing at a rate of about -1.75 per month. In other words, during the 20 month, around an additional -1.75 percent of the rats will die.
(b) Proceeding similarly to find f_c(20,6), we have f_c(20,6) \approx \frac{f(20,6+2) - f(20,6-2)}{4} = \frac{70 - 97}{4} = -2.07692, or, with one-sided difference quotients, f_c(20,6) \approx \frac{f(20,6+2) - f(20,6)}{2} = -2.22222 or f_c(20,6) \approx \frac{f(20,6) - f(20,6-2)}{2} = -1.75. These indicate that if the original concentration increases from 6 by 1 ppm, the percent surviving after 20 months decreases by about 2.08.

static.solution:

statement.p: Suppose that z is a linear function of x and y with slope -3 in the x direction and slope -4 in the y direction.
(a) A change of -0.2 in x and 0.1 in y produces what change in z?
change in z =
(b) If z=6 when x=2 and y=4, what is the value of z when x=2 and y=4.2?

static.solution:
(a) Since z is a linear function of x and y with slope -3 in the x direction, and slope -4 in the y direction, we have: z = -3 x - 4 y + c. We can write an equation for changes in z in terms of changes in x and y: \Delta z = (-3 (x + \Delta x) - 4(y + \Delta y) + c) - (-3 x - 4 y + c) = -3 \Delta x - 4 \Delta y. Since \Delta x = -0.2 and \Delta y = 0.1, we have \Delta z = -3 (-0.2) - 4(0.1) = 0.2. So a -0.2 change in x and a 0.1 change in y produces a 0.2 change in z.
(b) As we know that z=6 when x=2 and y=4, the value of z when x=2 and y=4.2 will be z = 6 + \Delta z = 6 - 3\Delta x - 4\Delta y. where \Delta z is the change in z when x changes from 2 to 2 and y changes from 4 to 4.2. We have \Delta x = 2 - 2 = 5.55111512312578e-17 and \Delta y = 4.2 - 4 = 0.2. Therefore, when x=2 and y=4.2, we have z = 6 - 3 \cdot(5.55111512312578e-17) - 4\cdot(0.2) = 5.2.

static.solution:
(a) The time in minutes to go 10 miles at a speed of s mph is (10/s)(60)= 600/s. Thus the 180 lb person going 10 mph uses (10.2)(600/10) = 612 calories, and the 200 lb person going 8 mph uses (7.9)(600/8) = 592.5 calories.
(b) The 180 lb person burns 612/180 = 3.4 calories per pound for the trip, while the 200 lb person burns 592.5/200 = 2.9625 calories per pound for the trip.

statement.p: At a certain point on a heated metal plate, the greatest rate of temperature increase, 4 degrees Celsius per meter, is toward the northeast. If an object at this point moves directly north, at what rate is the temperature increasing?
degrees Celsius per meter

solution.p: SOLUTION
Let T be the temperature function and P the point. The value of the greatest rate of increase is the magnitude of the gradient. Thus \left| \nabla T (P) \right| = 4.
The gradient points in the northeast direction, so \nabla T (P) = \left \langle 4 \cos (45^o) , 4 \sin (45^o) \right \rangle = \left \langle \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \right \rangle.

A unit vector in the north direction is \mathbf{u} = \langle 0, 1 \rangle, so the rate of change of increase of the temperature in that direction is D_{\mathbf u} T(P) = \nabla T (P) \cdot \mathbf{u} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}

Let f(x,y) = 4/x + 5/y + 6 x + 7 y in the region R where x, y > 0.
Explain why f must have a global minimum at some point in R (note that R is unbounded---how does this influence your explanation?). Then find the global minimum.
minimum =

static.solution:
f is continuous in the region R, but R is not closed and bounded so a special analysis is required.
Notice that f(x,y) tends to \infty as (x,y) tends farther and farther from the origin or tends toward any point on the x or y axis. This suggests that a minimum for f, if it exists, can not be too far from the origin or too close to the axes. For example, if x > 10 then f(x,y) > 6 x > 60, and if y > 10 then f(x,y) > 7 y > 70. If 0\lt x\lt 0.1 then f(x,y) > 4/x > 40, and if 0\lt y\lt 0.1 then f(x,y) > 5/y > 50.
Since f(1,1)=22, a global minimum for f if it exists must be in the smaller region R^\prime: 0.1 \le x \le 10, 0.1 \le y \le 10. The region R^\prime is closed and bounded and so have a minimum value at some point in R^\prime, and since that value is at most 22, it is also a global minimum for all of R.
Since the region R has no boundary, the minimum value must occur at a critical point of f. At a critical point we have f_x = -{4\over x^2} + 6 = 0 = f_y = -{5\over y^2} + 7 = 0. The only critical point is (\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}, \sqrt{\frac{5}{7}}), at which f achieves the minimum value f(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}},\sqrt{\frac{5}{7}}) = 2\sqrt{24} + 2\sqrt{35}

A closed rectangular box has volume 48\,\mbox{cm}^3. What are the lengths of the edges giving the minimum surface area?
lengths =

p.em: (Give the three lengths as a comma separated list.)

static.solution:
x,y, z cm. Then the volume is given by V = xyz = 48.
The surface area S is given by S = 2xy+2xz+2yz. Substituting z = 48/(xy) gives S = 2xy +\frac{96}{y} + \frac{96}{x}. At a critical point, \frac{\partial S}{\partial x} = 2y - \frac{96}{x^2} = 0, and \frac{\partial S}{\partial y} = 2x - \frac{96}{y^2} = 0.
The symmetry of the equations (or by dividing the equations) tells us that x=y and so that 2x - \frac{96}{x^2} = 0, so that x^3 = 48, \quad\mbox{and so}\quad x = 48^{1/3}\mbox{ cm}. Thus the only critical point is x = y = (48)^{1/3} cm, and z = 48/\left ( (48)^{1/3} \cdot (48)^{1/3} \right ) = (48)^{1/3} cm. At the critical point S_{xx} S_{yy}-(S_{xy})^2= \frac{192}{x^3}\cdot\frac{192}{y^3}-2^2= \frac{(192)^2}{x^{3}y^{3}}-4. Since D>0 and S_{xx}>0 at this critical point, the critical point x = y = z = (48)^{1/3} is a local minimum. Since S\rightarrow\infty as x,y\rightarrow\infty, the local minimum is a global minimum.

Substituting z = 52/(xy) gives S = xy + \frac{104}{y} + \frac{104}{x}. At a critical point \frac{\partial S}{\partial x} = y - \frac{104}{x^2} = 0, and \frac{\partial S}{\partial y} = x - \frac{104}{y^2} = 0.

At a critical point \frac{\partial S}{\partial x} = 2 x - y - 15 = 0, and \frac{\partial S}{\partial y} = 2 y - x = 0, so x = 2 y, and 2(2 y) - y - 15 = 0 giving y=5, so x=10 and z^2 = 204 - (10)(5) - 15 (10), so z=\pm 2. Design a rectangular milk carton box of width w, length l, and height h which holds 462 \text{ cm}^3 of milk. The sides of the box cost 2 \ \text{cents/cm}^2 and the top and bottom cost 4\ \text{cents/cm}^2. Find the dimensions of the box that minimize the total cost of materials used.
width = , length = , height =
(Include units in your answers.) ( )

solution.p: The total cost of the four sides is (2hl+2wh)(2) cents. The cost of top and bottom is (2wl)(4) cents. Thus the total cost C (in cents) of the box is C = (2)(2)(h)(l+w) + (2)(4) wl. The volume in \text{cm}^3 is wlh = 462, so w,l,h are nonzero and we may divide and obtain l = \frac{462}{wh}. Plug this into the equation for C to obtain \begin{aligned} C \amp = (2)(2)h\left(\frac{462}{wh} + w\right) + (2)(4)(w)\frac{(462)}{wh}\\ \amp =\frac{(2)(2)(462)}{w} + (2)(2)hw + \frac{(2)(4)(462)}{h} \end{aligned} as a function of h and w. To minimize C, find the critical points of C by solving 0=C_h = (2)(2) w - \frac{(2)(4)(462)}{h^2} hence 2 wh^2 = (4)(462), and 0=C_w = \frac{(-2)(2)(462)}{w^2}+(2)(2)h so w^2h = 462. The quotient of these two results is \frac{2 wh^2}{w^2h} = \frac{(4)(462)}{462} so 2 h/w = 4 and h = \frac{4}{2} w .

Plug that into the equation w^2h = 462 to obtain 4 w^3 / 2 = 462 so w^3 = \frac{(2)(462)}{4}, h^3 = \left(\frac{4}{2}\right)^3 w^3 = \frac{(4^2)(462)}{2^2} and, l^3 = \frac{461}{w^3 h^3} = \frac{(2)(462)}{4} = w^3. Hence w = l = \left(\frac{(2)(462)}{4}\right)^{1/3}\approx {6.13579}, and h = \frac{4}{2} w \approx {12.2716}, centimeters.

Next we check that these dimensions minimize the cost C. At the critical point we find that C_{hh} = \frac{(6)(4)(462)}{h^3} = \frac{(6)(2^2)}{4} C_{ww} = \frac{(6)(2)(462)}{w^3} = (6)(4) C_{hw} = (2)(2)
so

D=C_{hh}C_{ww}-C^2_{hw} = (6^2)(2^2)-(2^2)(2^2) > 0. So, at the critical point, D > 0 and C_{hh} > 0 hence C has a local minimum. Since C has no other critical points, and C increases without bound as (w,h)\to (0,0) and as (w,h)\to(\infty,\infty), this local minimum must be a global minimum.
Therefore, the dimensions of the box that minimize the cost are w=l \approx {6.13579}\ cm and h \approx {12.2716}\ cm.

statement.p: Use Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum and minimum values of f(x,y) = x - 2 y subject to the constraint x^2 + y^2 = 5, if such values exist.
maximum =
minimum =

p.em: (For either value, enter DNE if there is no such value.)

static.solution: f(x,y)= x - 2 y and our equation of constraint is g(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 = 5. To optimize f(x,y) with Lagrange multipliers we solve the following system of equations f_{x}(x,y) = \lambda g_{x}(x,y),\qquad\mbox{so } 1 = 2\lambda x, f_{y}(x,y) = \lambda g_{y}(x,y),\qquad\mbox{so } -2 = 2\lambda y, and g(x,y) = 5,\qquad\mbox{so } x^2 + y^2 = 5. Solving for \lambda gives us \lambda = \frac{1}{2 x} = \frac{-1}{ y}, which we can use to find x in terms of y: x = -\frac{1}{2}\,y. Using this relation in our equation of constraint, we can solve for y: x^2 + y^2 = 5, so (-\frac{1}{2}\, y)^2 + y^2 = 5, and thus ((\frac{1}{2})^2 + 1)\, y^2 = 5. So, solving for y, we have y = \pm 2, and x = \mp 1. Thus, the critical points are (-1,2) and (1,-2). Since the constraint is closed and bounded, maximum and minimum values of f subject to the constraint exist. Evaluating f at the critical points, we find that the maximum value is f(1,-2) = (1) + 2(2) = 5 and the minimum value is f(-1,2) = -(1) - 2(2) = -5.

statement.p: Use Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum and minimum values of f(x,y) = x^2 y + 3 y^2 - y, subject to the constraint x^2 + y^2 \leq 10
maximum =
minimum =

p.em: (For either value, enter DNE if there is no such value.)

static.solution:
f: f_x = 2xy = 0, \quad f_y = x^2 + 6 y - 1 = 0. From the first equation, we get either x=0 or y=0. If x=0, from the second equation we get 6 y - 1 = 0, so y=1/6. If instead y=0, then from the second equation x=\pm 1. We conclude that the critical points are (0,1/6), (1,0), and (-1,0). All three critical points satisfy the constraint x^2+y^2\le 10.
The Lagrange conditions, \nabla f= \lambda\nabla g, are: 2xy=\lambda 2x,\qquad x^2 + 6 y - 1 =\lambda 2y. From the first equation, when x\neq 0, we divide by 2x to get \lambda=y. Substituting into the second equation, we get x^2 + 6 y - 1 = 2y^2. Then using x^2 = 10 - y^2 from the constraint, we have 10 - y^2 + 6 y - 1 = 2 y^2, so 3 y^2 - 6 y - 9 = 0. Factoring, we get (3y + 3 )( y - 3 ) = 0, so y = -1 or y = 3. From the constraint, we get x=\pm 3 when y=-1 and x=\pm 1 for y=3.
If instead x=0, so that we cannot divide by x in the first Lagrange equation, then from the constraint, y=\pm \sqrt{10}.
Summarizing, the following points are either critical points or satisfy the Lagrange conditions: (\pm 1,0),(0,1/6),(\pm 3, -1),(\pm 1, 3), (0, -\sqrt{10}), \mbox{ and } (0, \sqrt{10}). These are the candidates for global maximum or minimum points. The corresponding values for f(x,y)=x^2 y + 3 y^2 - y are: 0, -0.083, -5, 27, 33.162, \mbox{ and } 26.838. The largest value is 33.1623 at the point (0,-\sqrt{10}), and the smallest value is -5 at (\pm 3,-1),

Find the minimum distance from the point (1,4,15) to the paraboloid given by the equation z=x^2+y^2.
Minimum distance =

Note: If you need to find roots of a polynomial of degree \geq 3, you may want to use a calculator of computer to do so numerically. Also be sure that you can give a geometric justification for your answer.

static.solution:
(x,y,z) be a point on the paraboloid. The square of the distance from (x,y,z) to the point (1,4,15) is given by f(x,y,z) = (x-1)^2 + (y-4)^2 + (z-15)^2, and so we wish to minimize f(x,y,z) subject to the constraint g(x,y,z) = x^2+y^2-z = 0. We look for solutions to the equations \nabla f = \lambda\nabla g and g=0: 2(x-1) = 2\lambda x, 2(y-4) = 2\lambda y, 2(z-15) = -\lambda, and x^2+y^2-z = 0. If \lambda=0, the first three equations would imply that (x,y,z)=(1,4,15), which does not satisfy the fourth equation and so \lambda\ne 0. If collect terms in x and y in the first and second equations, respectively, we get (1 - \lambda) x = 1, and (1 - \lambda) y = 4. Note that we cannot have \lambda = 1, x = 0 or y = 0, and so can divide these two equation to solve for y, getting y = 4 x.
If we divide the first and third equations we got from the Lagrange multipliers method, we have \frac{x - 1}{z - 15} = -2x, so that z = 15 - \frac12(1 - \frac{1}{x}).
We can then plug all of these into the last equation, the constraint. This gives x^2 + 16 x^2 - 15 + \frac12(1 - \frac{1}{x}) = 0. Multiplying by x and collecting terms, we have 34 x^3 - 29 x - 1 = 0. Let h(x) = 34 x^3 - 29 x - 1. Clearly h(-3) \lt 0, h(-\frac12) > 0, h(0) \lt 0 and h(3) > 0. Thus there must be roots lying between x = -3 and x = -0.5, between x = -0.5 and x = 0, and between x = 0 and x = 3. We can locate these numerically using a calculator or computer program, to find x = -0.90579834, \quad x = -0.03453103221, \quad\mbox{and}\quad x = 0.940329372. Then, using the equations for y and z in terms of x, we have the corresponding values of y and z, and therefore have three solutions to the Lagrange multiplier equations: x_1 = -0.90579834, y_1 = -3.62319336, z_1 = 13.9480007566948, x_2 = -0.03453103221, y_2 = -0.13812412884, z_2 = 0.020270667153297, and x_3 = 0.940329372, y_3 = 3.761317488, z_3 = 15.0317285733805.
The distances (squared) from the paraboloid are d_1 = d(x_1,y_1,z_1) = 62.8518467246095, d_2 = d(x_2,y_2,z_2) = 242.586616647641, and d_3 = d(x_3,y_3,z_3) = 0.0615366277493091, so that the minimum distance is \sqrt{d_3} = 0.248066.
Note that the geometric interpretation of this is that it is the length of a perpendicular line segment drawn from the paraboloid to the point.

statement.p: For each value of \lambda the function h(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 - \lambda(2 x + 6 y - 15) has a minimum value m(\lambda).

statement.p: (b) For which value of \lambda is m(\lambda) the largest, and what is that maximum value?
maximum m(\lambda) =
(c) Find the minimum value of f(x,y)=x^2+y^2 subject to the constraint 2 x + 6 y = 15 using the method of Lagrange multipliers and evaluate \lambda.
minimum f =

p.em: (How are these results related to your result in part (b)?)

static.solution:
(a) The critical points of h(x,y) occur where h_x(x,y) = 2 x - 2 \lambda = 0 and h_y(x,y) = 2 y - 6 \lambda = 0. The only critical point is (x,y) = ( \lambda, 3 \lambda) and it gives a minimum value for h(x,y). That minimum value is m(\lambda) = h( \lambda, 3 \lambda) = \lambda^2 + 9 \lambda^2 - \lambda( 2 \lambda + 18 \lambda - 15 ) or m(\lambda) = -10 \lambda^2 + 15 \lambda.
(b) The maximum value of m(\lambda)= -10 \lambda^2 + 15\lambda occurs at a critical point, where m'(\lambda) = -20 \lambda + 15 = 0. At this point, \lambda = 0.75 and m(0.75)= 5.625.
(c) We want to minimize f(x,y)=x^2+y^2 subject to the constraint g(x,y)=15, where g(x,y) = 2 x + 6 y. The method of Lagrange multipliers has us solve 2x = 2\lambda, 2y = 6\lambda, and 2 x + 6 y = 15. We can see that this gives the same solutions for x and y as we obtained in part (a), and then, plugging in to the third equation, we have 2 \lambda + 18 \lambda = 15. Thus we get the same \lambda as before: \lambda = 0.75, so that the minimum value of f is f(\lambda, 3\lambda), where \lambda = 0.75, or f_{\mbox{min}} = 5.625.
Note that the two question have the same answer. This makes sense, because in the first problem the largest minimum value will clearly occur when 2 x + 6 y = 15, which is the constraint in the third equation.

(a) If \sum_{i=1}^3 x_i = 2, find the values of x_1, x_2, x_3 making \sum_{i=1}^3 {x_i}^2 minimum.

p.em: (Give your values as a comma separated list.)

statement.p: (b) Generalize the result of part (a) to find the minimum value of \sum_{i=1}^n{x_i}^2 subject to \sum_{i=1}^n x_i=2.
minimum value =

static.solution:
(a) Let f(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\sum_{i=1}^3{x_i}^2 = {x_1}^2 + {x_2}^2 + {x_3}^2 and g(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\sum_{i=1}^3 x_i = 2. Then \nabla f = \lambda\nabla g gives 2x_1 = \lambda = 2x_2 = 2x_3. so x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = \frac{\lambda}2. Then x_1+x_2+x_3 = 2 gives 3\frac{\lambda}{2} = 2\quad\hbox{ so } \quad \lambda = \frac{4}{3}. Thus x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = \frac{2}{3}.
These values of x_1, x_2,x_3 give the minimum (rather than maximum) because the value of without bound as x_2,x_2,x_3\to\infty.
(b) A similar argument shows that \sum_{i=1}^nx_i has its minimum value subject to \sum_{i=1}^nx_i = 2 when x_1=x_2=\cdots= x_n=\frac{2}n. Then the minimum value is \sum_1^n \left(\frac{2}{n}\right)^2 = n\cdot \left(\frac{2}{n}\right)^2 = \frac{4}{n}.

Let R be the rectangle with vertices (0,0), (6,0), (6,6), and (0,6) and let f(x,y) = \sqrt{3xy}.
(a) Find reasonable upper and lower bounds for \int_{R}f\,dA without subdividing R.
upper bound =
lower bound =

(b) Estimate \int_{R}f\,dA three ways: by partitioning R into four subrectangles and evaluating f at its maximum and minimum values on each subrectangle, and then by considering the average of these (over and under) estimates.
overestimate: \int_{R}f\,dA \approx
underestimate: \int_{R}f\,dA \approx
average: \int_{R}f\,dA \approx

static.solution:
(a) If we take the partition of R consisting of just R itself, we get \mbox{Lower bound }= \mbox{min}_R f\cdot A_R=0\cdot (6-0)(6-0)=0. Similarly, we get \mbox{Upper bound } = \hbox{max}_R f\cdot A_R = 6\sqrt{3}\cdot (6-0)(6-0)=216\sqrt{3}.
(b) The estimates asked for are just the upper and lower sums. We partition R into subrectangles R_{(a,b)} of width 3 and height 3, where (a,b) is the lower-left corner of R_{(a,b)}. The subrectangles are then R_{(0,0)}, R_{(3,0)}, R_{(0,2)}, and R_{(2,2)}. Then we find the lower sum \mbox{Lower } =\sum_{(a,b)}A_{R_{(a,b)}}\cdot\min_{R_{(a,b)}}f = \sum_{(a,b)} 9\cdot (\mbox{Min of }f \mbox{ on }R_{(a,b)}). The minimum occurs at the lower-left corner of each rectangle, so \mbox{Lower } = 9\cdot( f(0,0) + f(3,0) + f(0,3) + f(3,3) ) = 108\sqrt{3}.
Similarly, the upper sum is \mbox{Upper } = 9\sum_{(a,b)}(\mbox{Max of }f \mbox{ on }R_{(a,b)}), so \mbox{Upper } = 9(f(2,2)+f(4,2)+f(2,4)+f(4,4)) = 27(3\sqrt3 + 2\sqrt{6}). The upper sum is an overestimate and the lower sum is an underestimate, so we can get a better estimate by averaging them to get 27(2\sqrt3 + \sqrt6).

R into subrectangles with the lines x=0, x=1, x=2, x=3, and x=4 and the lines y=0, y=0.75, y=1.5, y=2.25, and y=3. Then we have 16 subrectangles, each of which we denote R_{(a,b)}, where (a,b) is the location of the lower-left corner of the subrectangle.
We want to find a lower bound and an upper bound for the volume above each subrectangle. The lower bound for the volume of R_{(a,b)} is 0.75 ( \mbox{Min of } f \mbox{ on } R_{(a,b)}) because the area of R_{(a,b)} is 1\cdot 0.75=0.75. The function f(x,y) = 8+2xy increases with both x and y over the whole region R. Thus, \mbox{Min of } f \mbox{ on } R_{(a,b)} = f(a,b) = 8+2ab, because the minimum on each subrectangle is at the corner closest to the origin.
Similarly, \mbox{Max of } f \mbox{ on } R_{(a,b)} = f(a+1,b+0.75) = 8 + 2(a+1)(b+0.75). So we have \mbox{Lower sum } = \sum_{(a,b)} 0.75(8+2ab) = 0.75 \sum_{(a,b)} 8+2ab = 96 + 0.75\sum_{(a,b)}2 ab Since a=0, 1, 2, 3 and b= 0, 0.75, 1.5, 2.25, expanding this sum gives \mbox{Lower} = 96 + 0.75 (0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1.5 + 3 + 4.5 + 0 + 3 + 6 + 9 + 0 + 4.5 + 9 + 13.5) = 136.5.
Similarly, we can compute the upper sum: \mbox{Upper sum }= \sum_{(a,b)}0.75(8+2(a+1)(b+0.75)) = 0.75\sum_{(a,b)}(8+2(a+1)(b+0.75)) = 96 + 0.75\sum_{(a,b)}(a+1)(b+0.75) = 208.5.

We shall begin our sum as an upper estimate starting with the lower left corner of the room and continue across the bottom and moving upward using the highest temperature, T_i, in each case. So the upper Riemann sum becomes \sum_{i=1}^{25} T_i \Delta A = T_1 \Delta A + T_2 \Delta A + T_3 \Delta A + \cdots + T_{25} \Delta A = \Delta A (T_1 + T_2 + T_3 + \cdots + T_{25}). Thus, taking the maximum value for each region (and, where the temperatures are not bounded in the box, taking the largest value plus one), we have \mbox{sum} = (1)(20 + 21 + 21 + 22 + 22 + 21 + 22 + 22 + 22 + 23 + 23 + 23 + 24 + 24 + 24 + 24 + 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 + 26 + 27 + 28 + 27 + 26) = 592.
In the same way, the lower Riemann sum is formed by taking the lowest temperature (and, where the temperatures are not bounded in the box, taking the largest value minus one), t_i, in each case: \sum_{i=1}^{25} t_i \Delta A = t_1 \Delta A + t_2 \Delta A + t_3 \Delta A + \cdots + t_{25} \Delta A = \Delta A (t_1 + t_2 + t_3 + \cdots + t_{25}). Thus, taking the minimum value for each region, we have \mbox{sum} = (1)(17 + 19 + 20 + 21 + 21 + 19 + 20 + 21 + 21 + 22 + 21 + 21 + 22 + 22 + 22 + 22 + 23 + 23 + 24 + 24 + 23 + 24 + 25 + 25 + 24) = 546.
So, averaging the upper and lower sums we get: 569.
To compute the average temperature, we divide by the area of the room, \mbox{Average temperature} = \frac{569}{25} = 22.76. That is, approximately 22.76^{\circ}C.

static.solution:
(a) p is a joint density function. Since p(x,y)=0 outside the region R, the volume under the graph of p is the same as the volume under the graph of p over the region R, which is 1, not one, which it would have to be if p(x,y) were a joint density function..
(b) p is not a joint density function. Since p(x,y)=0 outside the region R, the volume under the graph of p is the same as the volume under the graph of p over the region R, which is 0.5, .
Finally, for a constant function to be a joint density function on R given by 0 \le x \le 2, 2 \le y \le 4, the volume under the constant must be one. So, if p(x,y) = k, 4 k = 1, so p(x,y) = \frac1{4}.

(b) x \lt \frac{1}{6} + y:
probability =

static.solution:
(a) The probability is \int_0^1\int_{1/6}^1 {2 \over 3} (x + 2y) \,dx\,dy = \int_0^1 {2\over3} ({1\over2}x^2 + 2xy)\bigr|^1_{1/6}\,dy = \int_0^1 {2\over3} \left[({1\over2} + 2y) - ({1\over 72} + {\frac{1}{3}}y)\right]\,dy = {2\over3}\int_0^1 (\frac{35}{72} + \frac{5}{3} y) \, dy = {2\over3} \left(\frac{35}{72} y + \frac{5}{6} y^2\right)\bigr|_0^1 = {2\over3} \left(\frac{95}{72}\right) = \frac{95}{108}.
(b) It is easier to calculate the probability that x \lt \frac1{6} + y does not happen, that is, the probability that x \ge \frac1{6} + y, and subtract it from 1. The probability that x \ge \frac1{6} + y is \int_{0}^{5/6}\int_{y+1/6}^{1} {2\over3} (x+2y) \,dx\,dy = \int_{0}^{5/6} (\frac13\,x^2 + \frac43\,xy) \bigr|_{y+(1/6)}^{1} \,dy = \int_{0}^{5/6} \frac13\left(1 - (\frac1{6} + y)^2\right) + \frac43(y)(1 - (\frac1{6} + y)) \,dy = \int_{0}^{5/6} -\frac53\,y^2 + y + \frac{35}{108} \, dy = (-\frac59\,y^3 + \frac{1}{2}\, y^2 + \frac{35}{108}\,y)\bigr|_{0}^{5/6} = \frac{575}{1944}. Thus, the probability that x \lt \frac1{6}+y is 1-(\frac{575}{1944}) = \frac{1369}{1944}.

static.solution: -\pi/4\le\theta\le\pi/4. Also, the outer (right) boundary of the region is \sqrt{8} = x = r\cos\theta. Hence, 0\le r\le \sqrt{8}/\cos\theta. The integral becomes \int_0^{\sqrt{8}}\int_{-x}^x\,dy\,dx =\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\int_0^{\sqrt{8}/\!\cos\theta}\,r\,dr\,d\theta. Then \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\int_0^{\sqrt{8}/\!\cos\theta}\,r\,dr\,d\theta = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\left(\frac{r^2}{2}\bigg|_0^{\sqrt{8}/\!\cos\theta}\right)\,d\theta = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{4}{\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta. And \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{4}{\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta =4 \tan\theta\bigg|_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = 4\cdot(1 - (-1)) = 8. Notice that we can check this answer because the integral gives the area of the shaded triangular region which is \frac{1}{2} \cdot \sqrt{8} \cdot (2\sqrt{8}) = 8.

static.solution:
z = 8 - 4 x - 2 y. Note that the projection of this into the xy-plane is the triangular region below y = 4 - 2 x.
The mass of the volume is then M = \int_R \delta\,dV = \int_0^2\int_0^{4 - 2 x}\int_0^{8-4 x-2 y}\,x + 4 y\,dz\,dy\,dx. Integrating with respect to z, M = \int_0^2\int_0^{4 - 2 x} (x + 4 y)(8-4 x-2 y)\,dy\,dx so that M = \int_0^2\int_0^{4 - 2 x} -4 x^2 + 8 x - 2 x y - 16 x y + 32 y - 8 y^2\,dy\,dx. Then, integrating with respect to y, M = \int_0^2 (-4 x^2 + 8 x)(4 - 2 x) + \frac12(32 - 18 x)(4 - 2 x)^2 - \frac{8}{3} (4 - 2 x)^3\,dx. Expanding the these terms, we have M = \int_0^2 \frac{-20}{3} x^3 + 48 x^2 - 112 x + \frac{256}{3}\, dx = 48.

statement.p: The moment of inertia of a solid body about an axis in 3-space relates the angular acceleration about this axis to torque (force twisting the body). The moments of inertia about the coordinate axes of a body of constant density and mass m occupying a region W of volume V are defined to be I_x = \frac{m}{V}\int_W (y^2+z^2) \,dV\qquad I_y = \frac{m}{V}\int_W (x^2+z^2) \,dV\qquad I_z = \frac{m}{V}\int_W (x^2+y^2) \,dV
Use these definitions to find the moment of inertia about the z-axis of the rectangular solid of mass 24 given by 0 \le x \le 3, 0 \le y \le 4, 0 \le z \le 1.

statement.p: Find the Jacobian. \frac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (s,t,u)}, where x = 4u-\left(3s+5t\right), y = 5s+5t+2u, z = -\left(5s+4t+4u\right).

static.solution: \left|\frac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (s,t,u)}\right| = \left|\begin{array}{ccc} x_s \amp x_t \amp x_u\\ y_s \amp y_t \amp y_u\\ z_s \amp z_t \amp z_u \end{array}\right| =\left|\begin{array}{ccc} -3 \amp -5 \amp 4\\ 5 \amp 5 \amp 2\\ -5 \amp -4 \amp -4 \end{array}\right|. This 3 \times 3 determinant is computed the same way as for the cross product, with the entries -3,-5,4 in the first row playing the same role as \vec i,\vec j,\vec k. We get \frac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (s,t,u)}= ((5)(-4)-(2)(-4))-3 + ((2)(-5)-(5)(-4))-5 + ((5)(-4)-(5)(-5))4 = 6.

Use the change of variables s=y, t=y-x^2 to evaluate \int\int_R x \,dx\,dy over the region R in the first quadrant bounded by y=0, y=9, y=x^2, and y=x^2-4.

static.solution:
dA=\,dx\,dy, the integrand x and the region R.
Inverting the variable change gives x=\sqrt{s-t}, y=s where we use the positive square root because the region R is in the first quadrant where x\ge 0. Thus \frac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (s, t)}= \left\vert \begin{array}{cc}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}\amp \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}\\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}\amp \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}\end{array}\right\vert =\left\vert \begin{array}{cc}1/(2\sqrt{s-t})\amp \quad -1/(2\sqrt{s-t})\\ 1\amp 0\end{array}\right\vert = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{s-t}}. Therefore dx\,dy = \left\vert \frac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (s, t)}\right\vert \,ds\,dt =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{s-t}} \,ds\,dt.
The integrand is x = \sqrt{s-t}.
The region of integration can be transformed by examination of its boundaries. The left and right boundaries of R are given by y-x^2=t=0 and y-x^2 = t =-4. The bottom and top boundaries of given by y=s=0 and y=s=9.
Let T be the rectangle 0\le s\le 9, -4\le t \le 0 of area (4)(9)= 36. We have \int\int_R x\,dx\,dy= \int\int_T \sqrt{s-t}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{s-t}} \,ds\,dt= \frac{1}{2}(\hbox{Area of T}) = 18.

statement.p: Use the change of variables s = x + 3 y, t = y to find the area of the ellipse x^2 + 6 x y + 10 y^2 \le 1.
area =

static.solution:
\int\int_R \,dx\,dy where R is the region x^2 + 6 x y + 10 y^2\le 1. We must change variables in both the area element dA=\,dx\,dy and the region R.
Inverting the variable change gives x = s - 3 t, y = t. Thus \frac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (s, t)}= \left\vert \begin{array}{cc} \frac{\partial x}{\partial s}\amp \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}\\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}\amp \frac{\partial y}{\partial t} \end{array} \right\vert = \left\vert \begin{array}{cr} 1 \amp -3\\ 0\amp 1 \end{array} \right\vert = 1. Therefore dx\,dy= \left\vert \frac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (s, t)}\right\vert \,ds\,dt = \,ds\,dt.
The region of integration is x^2 + 6 x y + 10 y^2 = (s - 3 t)^2+ 2(s - 3 t)t + 10 t^2 = s^2+t^2\le 1.
Let T be the unit disc s^2+t^2\le 1. We have \int\int_R \,dx\,dy= \int\int_T \,ds\,dt = \hbox{Area of }T = \pi.

statement.p: Use the change of variables s=xy, t=xy^2 to compute \int_R xy^2\,dA, where R is the region bounded by xy=3,\ xy=7,\ xy^2=3,\ xy^2=7.

static.solution:
\begin{array}{ccc}s\amp =\amp xy\\t\amp =\amp xy^2,\end{array}. we have \frac{\partial(s,t)}{\partial(x,y)}= \left| \begin{array}{ccc} \frac{\partial s}{\partial x} \amp \frac{\partial s}{\partial y}\\ \frac{\partial t}{\partial x} \amp \frac{\partial t}{\partial y} \end{array}\right| =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}y\amp x\\y^2\amp 2xy\end{array}\right|=xy^2=t. Since \frac{\partial(s,t)}{\partial(x,y)}\cdot \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}=1, \qquad \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}=\frac{1}{t}.
So \int_R xy^2\,dA=\int_{T}t\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right|\,ds\,dt= \int_{T}t\,(\frac 1t)\,ds\,dt=\int_{T}\,ds\,dt, where T is the region bounded by s=3, s=7, t=3, t=7. Then \int_Rxy^2\,dA=\int_3^{7}\,ds\int_3^{7}\,dt=16.

statement.p: Find positive numbers a and b so that the change of variables s=ax, t=by transforms the integral \int\int_R \,dx\,dy into \int\int_T \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert \,ds\,dt for the region R, the rectangle 0\le x \le 60, 0\le y \le 30 and the region T, the square 0\le s, t \le 1.
What is \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert in this case?

static.solution:
T is defined by the inequalities 0 \le s = ax \le 1 \qquad 0\le t=by\le 1 that correspond to the inequalities 0\le x \le 1/a = 60 \qquad 0\le y \le 1/b = 30 that define R. Thus a=1/60 and b=1/30.
Then, we have x = 60 s and y = 30 t, so \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert = \left|\begin{array}{cc} 60 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 30 \end{array}\right| = 1800.

statement.p: Find a number a so that the change of variables s=x+ay, t=y transforms the integral \int\int_R \,dx\,dy over the parallelogram R in the xy-plane with vertices (0,0), (28,0), (-36,8), (-8,8) into an integral \int\int_T \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert\,ds\,dt over a rectangle T in the st-plane.
What is \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert in this case?

static.solution:
x = s-at, y=t. The four edges of R are y=0, y=8, y=-\frac{2}{9} x, y=-\frac{2}{9} (x-28). The change of variables transforms the edges to t=0, t=8, t=-\frac{2}{9} s + \frac{2}{9} at, t=-\frac{2}{9} s + \frac{2}{9} at + \frac{56}{9}. These are equations for the edges of a rectangle in the st-plane if the last two are of the form: s=(\hbox{Constant}). This happens when the t terms drop out, or a=\frac{9}{2}. With a=\frac{9}{2} the change of variables gives \int\int_T \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert \,ds\,dt over the rectangle T: 0\le t \le 8, 0\le s\le 28.
The jacobian \left\vert\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert is \left\vert\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert = \left\vert\begin{array}{cc} 1 \amp -\frac{9}{2} \\ 0 \amp 1 \end{array} \right\vert = 1.

We therefore get \int_R (x+y) \,dA = \int_{T} ((5 s + t) + (s - 3 t)) \left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right|dsdt = \int_{T}(6s-2t)(16)\,ds\,dt=\int_{T} (16\mathopen{}\left(6s-2t\right))\,ds\,dt, where T is the region in the st-plane corresponding to R.

static.solution:
\vec G has its component in the x-direction given by (\mbox {curl }\vec G)_x \approx \frac{\mbox {Circulation around small square around } x \mbox {-axis}}{\mbox {Area inside square}} = \frac{\mbox {Circulation around }S_2}{\mbox {Area inside }S_2}= \frac{0.01}{(0.01)^2} = 100. Similar reasoning leads to (\mbox {curl }\vec G)_y\approx \frac{\mbox {Circulation around } S_3}{\mbox {Area inside }S_3}=\frac{0.04}{(0.01)^2}=400. and (\mbox {curl }\vec G)_z\approx\frac{\mbox {Circulation around } S_1}{\mbox {Area inside }S_1}=\frac{0.0001}{(0.01)^2}=1.
Thus, \mbox {curl }\vec G\approx 100\,\mathit{\vec i}+400\,\mathit{\vec j}+\,\mathit{\vec k}.

statement.p: Calculate \int_C \left(4 (x^2-y)\vec i + 8(y^2+x)\vec j\right) \cdot d\vec r if:
(a) C is the circle (x-8)^2+(y-8)^2=16 oriented counterclockwise.
(b) C is the circle (x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=R^2 in the xy-plane oriented counterclockwise.

static.solution:
(a) The curve, C, is closed and oriented in the correct direction for Green's Theorem. Writing A for the interior of the circle, we have \int_C \left( 4(x^2-y)\vec i +8(y^2+x)\vec j\right)\cdot d\vec r = \int_A \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}8 (y^2+x) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}4(x^2-y)\right) dx\,dy = \int_A (8-(-4))\, dx\,dy = 12 \int_A dx\,dy = 12\cdot \mbox{Area of }A = 192\pi.
(b) The circle given has radius R and center (a,b). The argument in part (a) works for any circle of radius R, oriented counterclockwise. So the line integral has the value 12\pi R^2.

static.solution:
(a) Since \vec F = 12 x e^{y}\,\vec i + 6 x^2 e^{y}\,\vec j is a gradient vector field and C is a closed curve, \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = 0.
(b) Since \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(6(x + y)) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(12(x - y)) = 18, by Green's Theorem,\int_C\vec G\cdot d\vec r = \int_R\left(18\right)\,dA = 18(\mbox{Area of triangle}) = 162.

solution.p: SOLUTION
Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C.

First note that the curve has a positive orientation. We will use Green's Theorem. We have P = 3 x - 2 y, \; Q = 4 x, therefore \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} =4+ 2 = 6 . Hence, Green's Theorem implies

p.m: \begin{array}{lcl} \int_{C} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r}\amp = \amp \iint_D \left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right) dA \\ \amp =\amp \iint_D 6 dA \\ \amp = \amp 6 \int_0^{\pi/4} \int_0^{3} r \, dr \, d\theta \quad \text{[Using polar coordinates]} \\\amp = \amp 6 \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \left(\frac{ 3^2}{2}\right) \\\amp =\amp {\frac{27}{4}} \pi \end{array}

statement.p: Let \vec F = (9 x^2 y + 3 y^3 + 3 e^x)\,\vec i + (2 e^{y^2} + 324 x)\,\vec j. Consider the line integral of \vec F around the circle of radius a, centered at the origin and traversed counterclockwise.
(a) Find the line integral for a=1.
line integral =
(b) For which value of a is the line integral a maximum?

p.em: (Be sure you can explain why your answer gives the correct maximum.)

static.solution:
(a) We use Green's Theorem. Let R be the region enclosed by the circle C. Then \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_R\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(2 e^{y^2} + 324 x) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(9 x^2 y + 3 y^3 + 3 e^x)\right)\,dA = \int_R 324 - 9(x^2 + y^2)\, dA. Converting to polar coordinates, we have \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 (324 - 9 r^2)r\,dr\,d\theta = 2\pi\left(162 r^2 - \frac{9}{4} r^4\right)\bigg|_0^1 = \frac{639}{2}\pi.
(b) The integrand of the integral over the disk R is 324 - 9(x^2+y^2). Since the integrand is positive for x^2 + y^2 \lt \frac{324}{9} = 36 and negative for x^2 + y^2 > 36, the integrand is positive inside the circle of radius 6 and negative outside that circle. Thus, the integral over R increases with a until a=6 and then decreases. The maximum value of the line integral occurs when a = 6.

static.solution:
S is parameterized by \vec r(r,\theta)=r\cos \theta\vec i+r\sin \theta\vec j+r\vec k, with 0\le r\le R and 0\le\theta\le 2\pi. We have \frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial r}\times \frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial \theta} = \left|\begin{array}{ccc} \vec i \amp \vec j \amp \vec k\\ \cos{\theta} \amp \sin{\theta} \amp 1 \\ -r\sin{\theta} \amp r\cos{\theta} \amp 0 \end{array}\right| = - r \cos\theta \vec i - r \sin \theta \vec j + r \vec k. Since the vector \partial \vec r / \partial r \times \partial \vec r / \partial \theta points upward, in the direction opposite to the specified orientation, we use d\vec A= -\left(\partial\vec r/\partial r\times\partial\vec r/\partial\theta\right) \,dr\,d\theta = (r\cos\theta\vec i + r\sin\theta\vec j - r\vec k)\, dr\,d\theta\,.
Hence \int_S\vec F\cdot d\vec A = \int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^R 8 (r^5 \cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta\vec k)\cdot (r \cos\theta \vec i + r \sin \theta \vec j - r \vec k)\,dr\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{R} -8 r^6\cos^2{\theta}\sin^2{\theta}\,dr\,d\theta = -\frac{8 R^7}{7}\int_0^{2\pi} \sin^2{\theta}\cos^2{\theta}\, d\theta = -\frac{8 R^7}{7}\int_0^{2\pi} \sin^2{\theta}(1-\sin^2{\theta})\, d\theta = -\frac{ 8 R^7}{7}\int_0^{2\pi} (\sin^2{\theta}-\sin^4{\theta})\, d\theta = -\left(\frac{8 R^7}{7}\right)\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)= -\frac{2}{7} \pi R^7.
The cone is not differentiable at the point (0,0). However the flux integral, which is improper, converges.

statement.p: Compute the flux of the vector field \vec F = z\vec i + 8 x\vec j through the parameterized surface S oriented upward and given, for 0\le s\le 1, \ \ 1\le t\le 2, by x=s^2, \quad y=2s+t^2, \quad z=1 t.
flux =

static.solution:
\partial \vec r / \partial s \times \partial \vec r / \partial t is given by \frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial s}\times\frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial t}= \left|\begin{array}{ccc} \quad\vec i\quad\amp \quad\vec j\quad\amp \quad\vec k\quad\\ 2s \amp 2 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 2t \amp 1 \end{array} \right| = 2\vec i- 2 s\vec j+4st\vec k. Since the z-component, 4st, of the vector \partial \vec r / \partial s \times \partial \vec r / \partial t is positive for 0 \lt s \leq 1, 1 \leq t \leq 2, we see that \partial \vec r/\partial s \times \partial \vec r / \partial t points upward, in the direction of the orientation of S we were given.
Thus, we use d\vec A = \left(\frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial s} \times \frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial t}\right)\,ds\,dt, and so we have \int_S\vec F\cdot d\vec A = \int_0^{1}\int_{1}^{2} (1 t\vec i + 8 s^2\vec j)\cdot (2\vec i- 2 s\vec j+4st\vec k)\,dt\,ds =\int_0^{1}\int_{1}^{2} (2 t - 16 s^3)\,dt\,ds = \int_0^{1}(1 t^2 - 16 s^3 t)\bigg|_{t=1}^{t=2}\,ds =\int_0^{1}(3 - 16 s^3)\,ds=(3s - 4 s^4)\bigg|_0^{1} =-1.

If S is the cube bounded by the six planes x = \pm 3, y = \pm 3, z = \pm 3, oriented outward, and \vec{F} = 2 \vec{i} - \vec{k}, then the flux of \vec{F} through S is zero.

If S is the unit sphere centered at the origin, oriented outward and the flux integral \displaystyle \iint_S \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{A} is zero, then \vec{F}(x,y,z) is perpendicular to \vec{r} = \langle x,y,z \rangle at every point of S.
