x=4 u+2, y=u-v, and z=7 u+v satisfy the equation of the plane, 2x-y-z =2(4 u+2 )-( u-v )-( 7 u+v )=8 u+4-u+v-7 u-v=4 Moreover, for any x, y, z satisfying 2x-y-z=4,
there are values of u and v such that x=4 u+2,
y=u-v, and z=7 u+v, since the following equations can be solved for u and v: \begin{array}{rcl}x\amp {}={}\amp 4 u+2\\ \noalign{\smallskip} y\amp =\amp u-v\\ \noalign{\smallskip} z\amp =\amp 7 u+v\\ \noalign{\smallskip} 2x-y-z\amp =\amp 4\end{array}\quad\Rightarrow\quad u=\frac{x-2}{4},\quad v=\frac{x-2}{4}-y We conclude that \mathrm{\Phi }( u,v ) parametrizes the whole plane 2x-y-z=4.
(a) The tangent vectors {\mathbf{T} }_u and {\mathbf{T} }_v are: {\mathbf{T} }_u =\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial u}=\frac{\partial }{\partial u}( 4 u+2,u-v,7 u+v )= \left\lt 4,1,7 \right>{\mathbf{T} }_v =\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial v}=\frac{\partial }{\partial v}( 4 u+2,u-v,7 u+v )= \left\lt 0,-1,1 \right> The normal vector is the following cross product: \mathbf{n} ( u,v )={\mathbf{T} }_u \times {\mathbf{T} }_v = \left|\begin{array}{rrr}\mathbf{i} \amp \mathbf{j} \amp \mathbf{k} \\ 4\amp 1\amp 7\\ 0\amp -1\amp 1\end{array}\right|=\left|\begin{array}{rr}1\amp 7\\ -1\amp 1\end{array}\right|\mathbf{i} -\left|\begin{array}{rr}4\amp 7\\ 0\amp 1\end{array}\right|\mathbf{j} +\left|\begin{array}{rr}4\amp 1\\ 0\amp -1\end{array}\right|\mathbf{k}= 8 \mathbf{i} -4 \mathbf{j} -4 \mathbf{k} = \left\lt 8,-4,-4 \right> (b) That area of S=\mathrm{\Phi }(\mathcal{D}) is the following surface integral: Area(S)=\iint_{\mathcal{D}} \| \mathbf{n} ( u,v )\| \,du \,dv=\iint_{\mathcal{D}} \| \left\lt 8,-4,-4 \right>\| \,du \,dv= 4\sqrt{6}\iint_{\mathcal{D}} 1 \,du \,dv=
4\sqrt{6}\, \mathrm{Area} (\mathcal{D}) =4\sqrt{6}\cdot 9\cdot 3=108 \sqrt{6} (c) We express f( x,y,z )=yz in terms of the parameters u and v: f\left(\phi ( u,v )\right)=( u-v )(7 u+v )=7 u^2-6 uv- v^2 Using the Theorem on Surface Integrals we have: \iint_S f( x,y,z ) \,dS = \iint_{\mathcal{D}}f\left(\phi ( u,v )\right)\| \mathbf{n} ( u,v )\| \,du \,dv=\iint_{\mathcal{D}} \left(7 u^2-6uv- v^2\right)\| \left\lt 8,-4,-4 \right>\| \,du \,dv= 4\sqrt{6}\int_0^{3} \int_0^{9} \left(7 u^2-6uv- v^2\right) \,du \,dv=4\sqrt{6}\int_0^{3} \left( \frac{7 u^3}3 -\frac{6u^2v}2- v^2u\right)\bigg|_{u=0}^{9} \,dv= 4\sqrt{6}\int_0^{3} \left(\frac{5103}3-\frac{486v}2-9 v^2\right) \,dv =4\sqrt{6}\left(\frac{5103v}3-\frac{486v^2}4-\frac{9 v^3}3 \right)\bigg|_0^{3} =\frac{188568\sqrt{6}}{12}\approx 38491.3

statement.p: Calculate \iint_{\mathcal{S}} f(x,y,z)\,dS For y = 4-z^2 \text{,} \qquad 0\le x, z\le 8 \text{;}\qquad f(x,y,z)=z \iint_{\mathcal{S}} f(x,y,z)\,dS=

static.solution: y=g( x,z ): \iint_S f( x,y,z ) \,dS=\iint_{\mathcal{D}} f\left(x,g( x,z ),z\right)\sqrt{1+ g_x^2+ g_z^2} \,dx \,dz \quad \mathbf{(1)} Since y=g( x,z )=4- z^2, we have g_x =0, g_z =-2z, hence: \sqrt{1+ g_x^2+ g_z^2}=\sqrt{1+4 z^2}f\left(x,g( x,z ),z\right)=z The domain of integration is the square \left[0,8\right]\times \left[0,8\right] in the xz-plane. By \mathbf{(1)} we get: \iint_S f( x,y,z ) \,dS = \int_0^{8} \int_0^{8} z\sqrt{1+4 z^2} \,dz \,dx=\left(\int_0^{8} 1 \,dx\right)\left(\int_0^{8} z \sqrt{1+4 z^2} \,dz\right)=8\int_0^{8} z \sqrt{1+4 z^2} \,dz We use the substitution u={1+4 z^2}, \,du= 8z \,dz to compute the integral. This gives: \iint_S f( x,y,z ) \,dS = 8\int_0^{8} z\sqrt{1+4 z^2} \,dz=8\int_1^{257} \frac{u^{1/2}}{8} \,du = \frac{16}3\cdot\left(\frac{{257}^{3/2}-1}{8}\right)\approx 2746.02

statement.p: Evaluate \displaystyle \int\!\!\int_{S} \sqrt{ 1 + x^{2} + y^{2} } \: dS where S is the helicoid: \mathbf{r}(u, v) = u\cos(v)\mathbf{i} + u\sin(v)\mathbf{j} + v\mathbf{k}, with 0 \leq u \leq 3, 0 \leq v \leq 2\pi

Find \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r where C is a circle of radius 2 in the plane x+y+z=2, centered at (1,2,-1) and oriented clockwise when viewed from the origin, if \vec F = 2y\vec i - x\vec j + 4\mathopen{}\left(y-x\right)\vec k

static.solution: \mbox{curl }\vec F = \left| \begin{array}{ccc} \vec i \amp \vec j \amp \vec k\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\ \amp \ \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \ \amp \ \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\\ 2y \amp -x \amp 4\mathopen{}\left(y-x\right) \end{array} \right| = 4\vec i + 4\vec j -3 \vec k, writing S for the disk in the plane enclosed by the circle, Stokes' Theorem gives \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_S\mbox{curl }\vec F\cdot d\vec A = \int_S(4\vec i + 4\vec j -3 \vec k)\cdot d\vec A. Now d\vec A = \vec n\,dA, where \vec n is the unit vector perpendicular to the plane and dA an area element on the plane, so \vec n = \frac1{\sqrt3}(\vec i + \vec j + \vec k), and \int_C\vec F\,d\vec r = \int_S(4\vec i+4\vec j -3\vec k)\cdot \frac{\vec i+\vec j+\vec k}{\sqrt{3}}\,dA = \int_S \frac{5}{\sqrt 3}\,dA = \frac{5}{\sqrt 3}\mbox{ Area of circle} = \frac{20\pi}{\sqrt{3}}.

statement.p: Consider the ellipse \left(\frac{x-6}{8}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{y + 3}{3}\right)^2 = 1 Find the equation of the ellipse translated so that its center is at the origin.

static.solution:
\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2} = 1 describes an ellipse with center (h,k).
Thus, for our ellipse to be located at the origin, it must have equation \frac{x^2}{{8}^2} + \frac{y^2}{{3}^2} = 1

statement.p: Find the equation of the ellipse with the given properties:
Foci (0, \pm 7) and two vertices at (\pm 2,0).

static.solution:
{\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{y}{b}\right)}^{2}=1.
The foci are \left(0, \pm c\right) on the y-axis with c=7, and two vertices are at \left(\pm a, 0\right) with a=2.
We use the relation c=\sqrt{{b}^{2}-{a}^{2}} to find b: b=\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{c}^{2}}=\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{7}^{2}} = \sqrt{53} Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is {\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{y}{\sqrt{53}}\right)}^{2}=1.

The conic section is
An ellipse
A Parabola
A hyperbola

(\pm \sqrt{42},0)
(0,0)
(\pm 49,0)
(0,\pm 49)
(\pm 7,0)
(0,\pm \sqrt{7})

The foci are at
(\pm 49,0)
(0,\pm \sqrt{42})
(\pm \sqrt{42},0)
(\pm 7,0)

The focal axis and the conjugate axis are
x=49 and y=7 respectively.
y=0 and x=0 respectively.
y=7 and x=49 respectively.
x=0 and y=0 respectively.

The conic section's center is at
(7,49)
(7,7)
(-7,-7)

static.solution:
49 to convert it to the equation in standard form: \frac{{x}^{2}}{49}+\frac{7 {y}^{2}}{49}=1 \Rightarrow \frac{{x}^{2}}{49}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{7}=1 \Rightarrow {\left(\frac{x}{7}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{y}{\sqrt{7}}\right)}^{2}=1 For this ellipse, a=7 and b=\sqrt{7} hence c=\sqrt{{7}^{2}-\left(\sqrt{7}\right)^2}=\sqrt{42}.
Since a>b we have:
\bullet The vertices are at \left(\pm 7, 0\right),\left(0, \pm \sqrt{7}\right).
\bullet The foci are {F}_{1}=\left(-\sqrt{42}, 0\right) and {F}_{2}=\left(\sqrt{42}, 0\right).
\bullet The focal axis is the x-axis and the conjugate axis is the y-axis.
\bullet The ellipse is centered at the origin.
